articles.summary: Isso significa que, a partir de 2027, a oposição poderá impor limites às decisões do presidente dos EUA e intervir em temas que afetam o mundo todo, como tarifas e a guerra no Irã.
articles.body:
O partido de oposição a Donald Trump obteve uma vitória histórica na eleição para o Congresso americano. Os democratas elegeram candidatos em estados que havia décadas não escolhiam um político do partido e conquistaram a maioria na Câmara e no Senado. Isso significa que, a partir de 2027, a oposição poderá impor limites às decisões do presidente Donald Trump e intervir em temas que afetam o mundo todo, como tarifas e a guerra no Irã. A correspondente Carolina Cimenti esteve em Austin, capital do Texas, um dos estados que fizeram parte dessa onda azul, que é a cor do Partido Democrata.

"O caso do Texas é um caso emblemático porque, há décadas, esse estado era a fortaleza do Partido Republicano. Há quase 40 anos, os texanos não elegiam um senador e alguém para o governo do estado do Partido Democrata, como aconteceu na noite de ontem. É um reflexo da mudança no perfil do texano, com o aumento da população latina e com uma participação muito maior dos jovens nessas eleições. 42% dos texanos hoje são hispânicos, são descendentes de latinos, e, por isso mesmo, a política de imigração do governo de Donald Trump, muito violenta contra os imigrantes latinos, principalmente, não caiu nada bem por aqui, e os eleitores levaram essa frustração para as urnas. Mas muitos texanos não imaginavam no tamanho da transformação que causariam. E essas mudanças não ficaram restritas somente aqui ao Texas. Elas aconteceram em vários estados no país todo, como mostra a nossa reportagem", diz Carolina Cimenti.

Menos de duas horas depois de as urnas fecharem no Texas, ficou claro: no estado onde o Partido Republicano domina o cenário político há mais de três décadas, os eleitores votaram na oposição em praticamente todos os cargos administrativos. E começaram as comemorações.

Além de Talarico, os democratas elegeram Gina Hinojosa como a primeira mulher latina governadora do Texas. Ela tirou do governo Greg Abbott, aliado de Donald Trump. O deputado democrata Al Green explicou o que estava acontecendo:

“O Texas é o coração dos estados republicanos. Se o batimento dele muda, então o país todo muda”.

A Jasmine, que votou nos democratas, disse:

“Queremos mudança. O preço da gasolina e de alimentos estão super altos. Estamos frustrados”.

Democratas vencem em redutos republicanos depois de décadas e conquistam maioria no Congresso — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Entre as causas do aumento do custo de vida estão a guerra no Irã e os tarifaços de Donald Trump. A frustração dos eleitores com o governo republicano não estava só no Texas e ela fez grupos que tinham apoiado Trump antes mudassem de voto e escolhessem a oposição. Entre eles, os mais jovens e também os latinos, que desaprovaram a política imigratória do presidente.

Essa frustração alimentou a onda democrata, que conquistou a maioria do Congresso americano. Os democratas tinham 45 das 100 cadeiras no Senado. Agora, terão pelo menos 54, contra 44 dos republicanos.

Os democratas conseguiram manter o controle de estados importantes - como Michigan e Georgia – e viraram sete estados que eram republicanos. No Kansas, há 94 anos o estado não elegia um senador democrata. O pastor Adam Hamilton venceu o atual senador Roger Marshall. Por lá, Trump perdeu apoio em áreas rurais, tradicionalmente republicanas. Os fazendeiros sentiram o impacto do tarifaço e da alta do combustível causada pela guerra no Irã. Um cenário parecido com o que aconteceu em Iowa. No Maine, a republicana Susan Collins ocupava a cadeira há 30 anos. O democrata Troy Jackson foi eleito para o lugar dela.

Na Câmara dos Deputados, os democratas ocupavam 214 cadeiras e os republicanos, 218. Agora, a oposição já soma 237 cadeiras, e as projeções indicam uma maioria ainda mais ampla. O deputado Hakeem Jeffries, democrata reeleito, que deve se tornar o presidente da Câmara, resumiu a noite da vitória:

“Não foi apenas uma onda azul. Foi um tsunami”.

articles.title: What Texas’ next governor has said about the border, illegal crossings
articles.summary: Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor's race Tuesday, defeating Gov. Greg Abbott.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor's race Tuesday. She has not said whether she will keep Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's Operation Lone Star, which she has been a critic of.

The border security program has seen Texas create its own border wall with Mexico and has sent more than 10,000 members of the National Guard to assist with security. It cost Texas more than $11 billion since its launch in 2021, two months into former President Joe Biden's term, according to Nexstar's Border Report.

Abbott conceded Tuesday night after calling to congratulate Hinojosa. Border counties that moved strongly to Trump in 2024 made up a large majority of votes that swung Texas toward Democrats this year.

What has Gina Hinojosa said about Texas' Operation Lone Star?

Hinojosa voted against the first round of appropriations for Operation Lone Star and has criticized Abbott for wasting taxpayer money to "grandstand" with it, according to Border Report , though she has not laid out an exact plan for its future.

"As governor, I'll put in the work to secure the border, not waste working Texans' money on political theater," she said in a news release.

What has Hinojosa said about immigration?

She's been clearest on her stance on the border wall plan for the Big Bend region, calling it unnecessary at a campaign stop in Presidio. Construction for the federal project is currently tied up in the courts.

Hinojosa has praised President Donald Trump for his immigration policy slowing illegal border crossings, while also criticizing ICE .

"Texas is the only state to detain little children and their parents because Greg Abbott made it happen," she said in a release. "Now we're seeing the deadly consequences of Abbott's corruption: American citizens killed by federal agents, law-abiding immigrants flown to Texas in violation of court orders, and children fed contaminated food in facilities that exist because Abbott chose profits over people. As governor, I will never offer up Texas as a staging ground for operations that terrorize families and enrich his donors."

articles.title: How a Democrat shocked the world in South Carolina
articles.summary: Annie Andrews turned a longshot into a real shot with money and outreach after Darline Graham replaced her late brother on the ticket.
articles.body:
As soon as Republican Sen. Darline Graham won the GOP nomination to replace her late brother in August, Democrat Annie Andrews made her move.

Andrews immediately began spending more than $5 million on advertising in South Carolina's Senate race at a moment when she largely had the airwaves to herself as her new opponent struggled to raise money. At the time, Republicans were racing to prioritize other competitive races across the country — and most people in both parties still saw South Carolina as a pipe dream for Democrats.

But by October, when the rest of the country began tuning into South Carolina — and spending money — Andrews had quietly become the frontrunner, according to internal campaign details shared with Semafor following her victory on Tuesday.

On Oct. 5, the Andrews campaign received a poll showing her with a 3-point lead over Graham. But the Democrat's campaign decided against publicly releasing the poll — or any subsequent internal poll — showing Andrews with a lead over Graham, wary of drawing too much attention from national Republicans and jeopardizing a peak at the right time, according to Chas Goldman, a strategist for Andrews.

That Republican attention did come, but not in time to save Graham in a state where Democrats hadn't won a Senate race since 1998. On a Senate map filled with shocking GOP losses, South Carolina stands out: It's the home of the National Republican Senatorial Committee chair, Tim Scott, and territory on which Democrats tried to compete statewide in 2020 — and lost handily.

Former GOP Rep. and Gov. Mark Sanford, R-S.C., told Semafor on Wednesday that he could feel the anti-Graham sentiment building on the state's coast but that most Republicans still felt that Graham could "nose it out" elsewhere. Ultimately, though, he said President Donald Trump's backing of Graham in a crowded primary which included Sanford and Reps. Ralph Norman and Russell Fry "never sat well with folks."

Sanford said Andrews did a good job appealing to disaffected Republicans but also said the rejection of Graham amounted to "a Waterloo moment for Trump."

"The fact that a state as red as South Carolina would go the other way on his hand-picked candidate? This is a person who said: 'Close your eyes and pretend you're voting for me.' OK, they did," Sanford told Semafor. "They just didn't like Darline as a candidate and felt it had been forced down their throats by Trump. And they're like: 'We're not doing this.'"

Andrews outran her party's gubernatorial nominee by 4 percentage points, evidence of both her strength and Graham's weakness as a candidate. Graham ran behind Alan Wilson, the Republican governor-elect, by roughly 100,000 votes.

In an interview with Semafor in early September, Andrews said she welcomed help from national Democrats and "anyone who wants to help me win this race, but I am confident I can do it without investment from the national party."

"I'm on TV, she's not up yet, and that's a huge advantage," Andrews said of Graham at the time. "All of the ingredients are in place, and I've been gifted with what is frankly an incredibly weak opponent. I'm ready."

Andrews exploited divisions in the Republican Party over Trump's endorsement of Graham, reaching out to supporters of Norman and former GOP Gov. David Beasley, according to details shared with Semafor.

She ran an ad with her Republican dad to appeal to former supporters of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham R-S.C., and worked with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., and other Black leaders in the state to juice turnout. Beasley ended up cutting a joint endorsement ad with former Democratic Gov. Jim Hodges while Norman's son, Warren, warmed publicly to Andrews.

By traditional campaign metrics, Andrews swamped Graham. She raised more than $25 million, according to her campaign, and was largely able to keep her own campaign afloat into October, when both national parties began spending in the race. Graham raised nearly $2 million, a sum that meant she would need outside support to win. Ultimately Democrats joined Andrews in the fray. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee quietly spent $500,000 there and Senate Majority PAC spent $750,000. Lauren French, a spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC, said that "Graham brought significant negatives and baggage to the race, that's undeniable, but Andrews won this race as much as Graham lost it."

Sen. Raphael Warnock, from neighboring Georgia, campaigned for Andrews, but she mostly sought to keep the campaign local. Her coattails extended to a House pickup in the state's lowcountry as she targeted Republicans and independents in her campaign events.

"For 18 months, she traveled all 46 counties, earning voters' trust one conversation at a time. She worked just as hard to raise the resources to go up on TV early and stay there. Those relationships and that early investment built a lead that she never gave up," said Brexton Isaacs, Andrews's campaign manager.

I interviewed Andrews throughout this saga: Once when she launched, once earlier this year when it appeared Lindsey Graham would be her opponent, and once after Darline Graham replaced her brother on the ticket. Each time she explained to me why this wasn't like 2020, when Jaime Harrison raised gobs of money but lost to Lindsey Graham.

I was as skeptical as anyone else that South Carolina was ready to elect a Democrat to the Senate. But over the last couple weeks, the whole country tuned in as national Republicans and Democrats alike poured money in. At the moment it's the biggest surprise on the Senate map — perhaps until we find out what happens in Mississippi.

Graham began thinking about running for a full term in July after discussing it with President Trump, Semafor reported.

articles.title: Florida Gov-elect Donalds believes 'frustrations boiled over' against Republicans on Election Day
articles.summary: Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., following the midterm elections, says there is a "frustration out there that we have a responsibility to address."
articles.body:
Florida Governor-elect Byron Donalds told Fox News on Wednesday that he believes Americans' frustrations about gas and diesel prices "boiled over" against Republicans on Election Day.

The Trump-backed Florida House Republican made the remark after being asked by "Fox & Friends" co-host Brian Kilmeade why he thinks so many people were unhappy with the first two years of the president's second term. The Democrats took back control of the House and Senate during the midterms , including flipping governor seats in states such as Texas, Georgia and Ohio.

"I think, look, when you talk to people on the ground, gas prices are a major problem. I think people were looking at the price of gas, the price of diesel, and I think those frustrations boiled over," Donalds said.

"I also want to look at, you know, in the United States Senate, there were some opportunities I think that were missed: not passing a Save America Act, not getting some of the key policies done, like putting through President Trump's border security packages and codifying that into law. I think that stuff frustrated Republicans," he continued.

"I think if you not just look in Florida, but look around the country, what I'm starting to see is that we have a lot of Republicans who either did not vote or decided to go and vote for Democrats. And I think there's a frustration out there that we have a responsibility to address," Donalds added. "And that's something I'll be talking about with my colleagues on Capitol Hill when I get back during this lame duck session. We're also going to be laser-focused on that here in Florida moving forward."

Donalds attributed his success in the Sunshine State to a robust ground game, noting that his campaign knocked on over 2.2 million doors and centering his election effort "on the issues that mattered to Floridians: insurance costs, housing costs, making sure kids were getting the best education possible."

"I got to give a thanks to the people of Florida all throughout the state for supporting us. The people in the Panhandle, the Panhandle once again kept Florida as a conservative state. So we're very grateful to the voters in the Panhandle," Donalds told "Fox & Friends."

"But we also want to talk to all the people of Florida. We have a mission. The campaign was not talking points. We are going to make Florida more affordable for the people of our state. We're going to make sure that our kids can achieve their Florida dream here in Florida," he added. "It was a tough fought victory last night. But we were able to win and be decisive. And now we get to the job of making sure that our state works for everybody."

Donalds made history by becoming the first Black politician to win a gubernatorial election in Florida and the first Black Republican in the nation's history to be elected governor.

Donalds, a three-term representative from Southwest Florida, defeated Democratic rival former Rep. David Jolly.

Donalds was endorsed by Trump in February of last year before he even formally launched his campaign for governor.

Fox News' Paul Steinhauser and Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

articles.title: Fox News Voter Poll: How Democrats took control of the Senate
articles.summary: Democrats flipped Senate seats across red and blue states as President Donald Trump's approval, inflation and gas prices dragged down GOP candidates.
articles.body:
The much-touted "blue wave" came to fruition as Democrats won a stunning run of victories in both red and blue states.

They also came out ahead in key governor's races.

The Fox News Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters nationwide, highlights the central themes and demographic groups that defined these important races.

Democrat Annie Andrews won a close-run race against incumbent Republican Darline Graham to flip a Senate seat that had been in the hands of Graham's brother Lindsey for more than 20 years.

Appointed to the seat after her brother's death in July, Graham underperformed his electoral strength; he won re-election to the Senate in 2020 by 11 percentage points. She also underperformed President Donald Trump's strength among key groups from two years ago.

Rural voters, for instance, backed Trump with 63% in 2024 – Graham this year garnered only 51%. Former Vice President Kamala Harris received 36% of the rural vote in 2024; Andrews bested that by about 10 points.

Graham did manage to hang on to non-MAGA Republican voters, amid concerns that they would defect. But again, she got 70% of their vote, while Trump pulled in 79% two years ago.

Independents: Andrews ran away among these voters, getting about 7 in 10. Trump received 39%, while Graham managed less than 20%.

Andrews did well with women, college graduates and urban voters.

She also benefited from Democrats being more unified behind her than Republicans were for Graham. Almost all Democrats backed Andrews, while just about 8 in 10 Republicans voted for Graham. More than 10% of Republicans crossed party lines to support Andrews.

The economy was by far the top issue in the state, with more than four in 10 putting it in the top spot. Andrews received the majority of those voters.

Three-quarters said inflation caused their family hardship in the past year, and more than half are very concerned about the cost of gas, food, utilities and healthcare.

And voters blame Trump for their economic woes: six in 10 say his policies have made things worse, and more than half blame him for inflation.

Graham was also found lacking as far as having the right experience to serve as senator. More than six in 10 said she did not.

Democrat Sherrod Brown won back his seat in the Senate, flipping it into the "D" column. He was ahead in the polls throughout the race and pulled off a win against Republican Jon Husted, who had been appointed to JD Vance's seat when he became vice president.

Husted tried to play the "extreme" card on Brown, which didn't quite play among an electorate that was familiar with him after serving three terms in the Senate. More than half said he wasn't.

Brown did, on the other hand, wield the too-close-to-Trump card on Husted – and quite effectively at that, with close to six in 10 voters saying the Republican was too supportive of the president.

The question of whether Democrats could regain working-class voters amid concerns over the economy and affordability was at the heart of this race. And it appears they did.

Husted struggled with working-class voters. Two years ago, Trump pulled in 61% of voters with no college degree – Husted got only half.

Trump also dominated among rural voters two years ago, garnering 70%; Husted was about 11 percentage points below that.

Young voters: Trump pulled in 60% of voters under 30 in 2024; Husted, not even a quarter. That is an enormous swing to Brown and the Democrats.

Hispanic voters were another huge swing back into the Democratic column. Trump got 58% to Harris' 41% in 2024. This time, three-quarters of them went for Brown.

The economy was definitely at the top of voters' minds. Close to seven in 10 say the state of the economy is not good, eight in 10 say inflation has been a hardship for them, and six in 10 say Trump's policies are to blame.

Add that up, and Trump was no doubt a drag on Republican Husted. The president's job approval is underwater by close to 20 points.

Six in 10 also say that Trump prioritizes his own interests rather than the country's.

In the end, it was a tough year to run as a Republican – even in a traditionally Republican state – when the party's president is unpopular and people are worried about their finances.

Finally, the top quality Ohio voters say they are looking for in a senator is change. And Brown is apparently that guy, with half of those voters backing him compared to about four in 10 for Husted.

The Ohio governor's race was competitive, but ended in the "D" column as well. A controversial ad by the Vivek Ramaswamy campaign attacking Democrat Amy Acton appears to have had little impact, with voters who made their decision in the last week, basically breaking even between the two candidates.

Five-term Sen. Susan Collins was the only Republican member of Congress from New England – and that total is now down to zero after first-time candidate Troy Jackson, a former logger and Maine Senate president, defeated the Vacationland mainstay.

The race was tight throughout, but Democrats spent a lot of time tying Collins as closely as they could to President Trump, who is not very popular among Maine voters . Six in 10 disapprove of the job he is doing.

That seems to have had an effect, with six in 10 saying she is too supportive of the president.

Who controls the Senate was a big concern for Maine voters, with eight in 10 saying it was a crucial or major factor to their vote. Jackson carried those voters by more than 10 points.

The state of democracy was the number one issue for Maine voters. And these voters went eight in 10 for Jackson.

Three-quarters are angry or dissatisfied with the direction the country is going; again, those voters went overwhelmingly for Jackson.

The quality Mainers said they'd most like to see in their senator is the ability to bring needed change. Those voters went big for Jackson.

Jackson bested Collins among women, young voters, college graduates, liberals, urban and suburban voters.

One of Collins' strongest groups was non-MAGA Republicans, which was pretty much her brand. But not enough to carry the day.

Trump won Iowa by 13 percentage points in 2024, but two years later, Republican Ashley Hinson was edged out by Democrat Josh Turek, who flipped the seat currently held by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst.

Hinson managed to hang on to rural voters, but not by as much as Trump did two years ago, and that could have been a key factor in the race, with rural Republican voters feeling hampered by tariffs, high gas and diesel prices and the Iran war.

Six in 10 voters say tariffs are hurting Iowa's economy, the same number who say they are very concerned about the price of gas, and the same number yet again who say the Iran war, a major cause of high gas prices, was the wrong decision.

Iowa voters are not happy with the way things are going in the country, to say the least, with seven in 10 angry or dissatisfied about it.

Iowans don't approve of the job Trump is doing, and Hinson likely paid a price for that, with more than half saying she is too supportive of him.

In the end, Turek's strength among young voters and Hispanics – two groups Trump did very well with only two years ago – plus college graduates and suburban voters was all too much for Hinson to overcome.

What seemed a safe bet turned into a surprisingly tough re-election bid for Kansas Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who lost to popular megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton in a flip for the Democratic column.

Kansas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly 100 years. But Hamilton, being a well-known figure in the state, plus the headwinds of a tough economy and an unpopular president facing Marshall, was able to change that.

The price of gas was a big concern for Kansas voters, a fact Marshall himself acknowledged during the campaign. And indeed, more than half of them said they were very concerned about it.

The war in Iran, one of the causes of those high gas prices, was another concern, with six in 10 saying it was the wrong decision, and more than nine in 10 saying it was a factor in their vote.

Tariffs were another key issue in a farm state, with six in 10 saying they are hurting the Kansas economy.

Rural voters backed Trump 72% two years ago, but only about six in 10 did the same for Marshall.

Trump overall was not a help for Marshall, even though he campaigned for him in the state three times. His job approval is underwater by more than 10 points, and Marshall made no attempt to distance himself from the increasingly unpopular president.

That likely hurt him in the end, as six in 10 Kansas voters point the finger at Trump's policies for inflation and for worsening economic conditions.

They also think Trump has taken his eye off the ball when it comes to what matters, with close to six in 10 saying the president is focusing on the wrong priorities. Those voters went almost 10 to one for Hamilton.

In addition to rural voters, Marshall also underperformed rather spectacularly with young voters, who gave Trump 58% of the vote in 2024, but went more than eight in 10 for Marshall's opponent, Hamilton.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed pulled off a win against Republican Rep. Mike Rogers to keep Michigan's Senate seat blue. He will be the first Muslim member of the Senate.

El-Sayed fended off charges of family ties to extremist groups and being too closely aligned with the far-left during the campaign. But when asked whether they found him too extreme, Michigan voters said no.

His opponent Rogers, however, faced the headwinds of an unpopular president of his own party with some policies that were pretty unpopular in the state he was hoping to represent. When asked if he was too closely tied to Trump, the answer was a resounding yes – with more than six in 10 saying so.

Michigan voters really don't like the job Trump is doing – six in 10 say they disapprove. Seven in 10 say the economy is in bad shape, eight in 10 say inflation has been a hardship for them, while four in 10 say their family's financial situation has gotten worse over the past year. All of these voters broke for El-Sayed.

Israel became an issue in the campaign, with more than half saying U.S. support is too strong.

There was concern that Black voters wouldn't come through for El-Sayed, but close to nine in 10 of them did, about the same level as they did for Harris in 2024.

Young voters: half of them went for Trump two years ago in Michigan. This time, less than a third backed Rogers.

Rogers did well enough with rural voters and those with no college degree, reliably Republican groups. But he couldn't overcome El-Sayed's strength among women, college graduates, urban and suburban voters.

In a race that seemed surprisingly close in a reliably blue state, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan succeeded in holding retiring Sen. Tina Smith's seat for the Democrats.

Her opponent, longtime NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, tried to hit Flanagan hard on corruption, linking her to the massive fraud scandals unfolding in the state. And corruption is indeed a major concern for voters, with six in 10 saying it is a major problem. Those voters went more than two to one for Tafoya, but Flanagan carried the day just about everywhere else.

The top issue in Minnesota is the state of democracy. Flanagan carried those voters by four to one.

The economy was the No. 2 issue for Minnesota voters, and they are clearly not happy with any of it. Seven in 10 rate the economy as not so good or poor, eight in 10 say inflation has been a hardship for their family, six in 10 blame Trump's policies for inflation, and two-thirds say Trump policies have made the economy worse.

Flanagan worked overtime to link Tafoya to the unpopular president, and it seems to have paid off. Voters also question Tafoya's experience, with more than half deciding she didn't have enough.

Flanagan's far-left progressive politics don't seem to give them pause, however, with more than half saying her views are not too extreme.

James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, flipping a Senate seat in a state Trump won by 14 points only two years ago and breaking a decades-long Republican hold on the Lone Star State. He is the first Democrat in more than 30 years to win a statewide race in Texas.

Hispanic voters, who gave half of their vote to Trump in 2024, turned around and supported Talarico by two-thirds.

Young voters turned out overwhelmingly for Talarico, with eight in 10 backing him – this after more than half of them supported Trump two years ago.

Trump carried 73% of rural voters in 2024. Talarico didn't win them, but Paxton struggled with this die-hard Republican group, getting about six in 10 of their votes.

Paxton also held on to three quarters of non-MAGA Republicans, many of whom were expected to defect, but gave him about the same level of support as they did Trump in 2024.

Paxton was a controversial candidate, having won a divisive primary against longtime Republican Sen. John Cornyn and facing various legal and personal scandals. His unfavorable rating reflects this, with six in 10 saying they don't have a good opinion of him. Four in 10 say the same about Talarico.

Black support was crucial for Talarico, especially after his own divisive primary against Rep. Jasmine Crockett, who did not endorse him. And turn out they did – nine in 10 of them. This after Trump managed to pull 20% of the Black vote in 2024.

Texas voters are in an ornery mood, with seven in 10 saying they are angry or dissatisfied with the direction the country is going.

They're also feeling surly about the Iran war – perhaps not a surprise in a state so dependent on the oil business. Nine in 10 say the war was a factor in their vote, six in 10 say it was the wrong decision, and another six in 10 say they are very concerned about the cost of gas.

In the governor's race, Republican Greg Abbott was seeking a historic fourth term, but lost to Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, who will be the first Hispanic governor of the state and the first Democrat elected governor since Ann Richards in 1990.

Abbott's loss is perhaps not surprising given more than half of Texas voters have an unfavorable opinion of him, compared to about four in 10 who feel the same way about Hinojosa.

In a race featuring the incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan, Democrat Mary Peltola, and independent "Decoy" Dan Sullivan, the Alaska Senate race remains too early to call at the end of the night.

The focus of the final week of the campaign turned on a New York Times report saying Alaska Democrats intentionally placed a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot in order to hurt the Republican's chances. Peltola denied the report, but lawsuits and accusations were flying as voters headed to the polls.

As elsewhere across the country, affordability issues were a key concern. Just about half of Alaska voters were very concerned about the cost of gas, healthcare, food and utilities.

The economy was not the No. 1 issue, however. The state of democracy took top place, and those voters went strongly for Peltola.

Trump carried the state by 13 points in 2024. Now, more voters disapprove of the job he's doing than approve.

Two years later he's not exactly a help. More than half say that Sullivan is too close to the president. Yet, almost one in five of those who say he is too supportive of Trump still back him.

The Fox News Voter Poll is based on a survey conducted by SSRS with registered voters nationwide. This survey was conducted Oct. 19 to Nov. 3, 2026, concluding at the end of voting on Election Day. It includes more than 900 interviews with voters in South Carolina; 1,000 in Kansas; 2,900 in Alaska; 4,000 in Maine; 3,900 in Minnesota; 4,300 in Ohio; 4,400 in Iowa; 4,700 in Michigan; and 5,200 in Texas. Full methodological details are available here.

articles.title: Florida DeSantis describes GOP midterms wipeout as 'close to an extinction-level event' for Republicans
articles.summary: Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called the midterm elections results a "close to an extinction-level event" for Republicans around the U.S.
articles.body:
Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Wednesday that the Republican losses in the midterm elections are "close to an extinction-level event" for the party "in many parts of the country, as we have seen probably in the last 100 years."

DeSantis spoke after Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate on Election Day. Rep. Byron Donalds, a Florida House Republican, won the contest for DeSantis' seat despite other GOP candidates losing their gubernatorial races around the U.S.

"Here's the thing. Democrats are unpopular. They were able to win based off the sentiment that exists in the country right now. They did not earn a mandate to indulge all their left-wing fantasies. And they're going to be in there governing, and we'll see what ends up happening," DeSantis said.

"But this was not a positive view of the Democrats. This was a rejection of Republicans in Washington," he added. "And Democrats just happened to be the beneficiary."

DeSantis, who has not ruled out a 2028 presidential bid, said, "In January, when everyone in office leaves, who were either term-limited or got voted out of the 10 largest states in this union, only one state will have Republican control of their state, the state of Florida.

"Last night we witnessed — to call it a wave, I don't think would be fully accurate — it's the political equivalent of a meteor strike that went all around the United States. Blue states, red states, everything in between," DeSantis said. "And the one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of Florida.

"If you look at our chief rival, in a healthy sense, the state of Texas, and I would say over my lifetime, Texas has been the crown jewel of Republican politics. I think we've been the leader for Republicans and conservatives since I've been governor. But if you go over the whole generation, no one holds a candle on the Republican side to the Lone Star State. And yet, not only did they lose a very highly publicized U.S. Senate race, they lost everything," DeSantis continued.

"The governor, attorney general, all the other statewide. They lost four Republican Supreme Court justices on the Texas Supreme Court. They may even lose the Texas Legislature or one house or even both. Let's just be clear that that is going to hurt, not just for the next two years. That's something that can reverberate for the next decade or more," he also said. "And if the Republican Party doesn't have Texas as an anchor, then we are not going to be viable nationally going forward."

DeSantis predicted that in the 2028 election cycle, "You are not, as Republicans, going to be able to retake the Senate under this current map just two years from now.

"And with all the House seats that have been done, probably not viable to take that back as well. So this is really going to have an impact," DeSantis added. "Two years, four years, six years, maybe even longer before Republicans could exercise unified control in Washington again like we've enjoyed over the last two years."

articles.title: GOP's midterm defeat sparks bold claims from foreign leaders who've clashed with Trump
articles.summary: Pedro Sánchez says Americans voted against hate and climate denial as European leaders react to the Democratic Party's 2026 midterm victories.
articles.body:
The GOP's sweeping midterm losses are drawing a positive response from several foreign leaders who have clashed with President Donald Trump, with some expressing hope that Democrats' victories could lead to a shift in U.S. policy on major global issues.

Democrats secured majorities in both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate in Tuesday's elections, setting the stage for a shift in congressional power in January and prompting reactions from officials in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez took aim at Trump's policies in a Wednesday X post, suggesting that American voters had rejected the president's political agenda and predicting that a similar shift would soon take place in Spain.

"Yesterday, American society voted against policies that only make people poorer," Sánchez wrote. "Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denial and against elite privilege."

Sánchez has been an outspoken critic of U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran, accusing Washington in March of "playing Russian roulette" with millions of lives. His opposition to the war and disputes with Trump over NATO defense spending have contributed to tensions between Madrid and Washington.

"We are not going to be complicit in something that is bad for the world and is also contrary to our values and interests, just out of fear of reprisals from someone," Sánchez said.

"Wild result in the USA last night! I'm cautiously optimistic on Europe's behalf," European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose wrote in a Wednesday X post. "Not because everything now changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and relations with the rest of the world."

Schaldemose criticized Trump's interest in Greenland in January 2025, also suggesting that Europeans should "stand up for ourselves both in terms of the economy the global economy but also in terms of digital policy and the climate."

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that the election results presented an opportunity for world leaders to work together to ease cost-of-living pressures and resolve the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, Sky News reported.

"Well, President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all - and that's the cost-of-living," Burnham said. "That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we've made moves, but I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved."

Trump said in July that he had a "very good" conversation with Burnham about trade and security issues, although the two governments have since differed over Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank. In September, Britain announced plans to strengthen sanctions targeting settlements and prevent British companies from assisting settlement construction, drawing criticism from U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee.

Americans have been grappling with higher costs as the war in Iran has caused energy prices to surge . The U.S. affordability crisis was a major issue for voters heading into this year's midterms.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad ‌Baqer Ghalibaf claimed in a Wednesday social media post that U.S. voters "said NO TO WAR" amid cost-of-living concerns.

"Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Ghalibaf said, according to the Independent. "If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."

Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara emphasized during a Wednesday press conference that the Japan-U.S. alliance "remains the cornerstone of Japan's foreign and security policy regardless of the outcome of the elections," Kyodo News reported .

Additionally, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told reporters on Wednesday that he thinks the Democratic Party's victory in the midterms will "introduce a new era in world relations," Reuters reported .

Trump confronted Ramaphosa during a May 2025 White House meeting, playing video footage that he claimed showed evidence of widespread violence against White South African farmers. Ramaphosa disputed Trump's allegations of persecution, while subsequent fact-checks found that some of the footage had been mischaracterized.

Trump claimed in a Tuesday night Truth Social post that if his name appeared on the ballot in the 2026 midterms the GOP would have "won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

Trump nevertheless congratulated Democrats on their victories and expressed a willingness to work with the incoming congressional majorities, while emphasizing that he would retain the power to veto legislation he opposes.

"They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier on Tuesday night, adding that the two parties would eventually have to work together to get legislation passed.

articles.title: Trump touts ‘magnificent’ ballroom in first remarks after midterm drubbing
articles.summary: President Trump, in his first public remarks since Republicans lost big in the midterm elections, showed off the White House ballroom construction Wednesday....
articles.body:
President Trump, in his first public remarks since Republicans lost big in the midterm elections , showed off the White House ballroom construction Wednesday.

The president signed the final beam, along with workers and other officials, and watched it get lifted into place. He didn't mention the results of the midterm elections until taking questions from reporters, when he also remarked on Vice President Vance's statement that the Iran war cost Republicans the midterms.

Trump called the ballroom "the most powerful building structurally … they say ever built and it was designed that way so the president can have safety," Trump said. "It's been the dream of presidents to have a ballroom for 150 years."

He said it is ahead of schedule and under budget, which he has said many times.

"When I get criticized, like, 'Why are you working on the White House?' I'm doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America," he said. "And it's got to be pristine. It's got to be perfect. And if you take a look at it, that's what it is right now."

"Just this whole magnificent space will be a very important space in the future life of our country," he said.

He also talked about the planned Triumphal Arch, the new helipad on the White House's North Lawn, the planned National Garden of American Heroes and his renovation of the East Potomac Golf Links.

When asked about Vance's statement on social platform X, Trump said, "I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term."

He said he thought the war was "worth it."

"I mean, well, you have no choice," he said.

The midterm elections came out in the Democrats' favor, flipping seats to take control of both the House and Senate.

He said he would "get along probably" with the Democrats "unless they want to be destructive."

"But I have the power of the veto," he said, adding that he has already spoken with some Democrats.

He said he would "stay out of" the race to pick a new House Republican leader after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said he would not run .

articles.title: Majority Leader Thune says Senate GOP won't 'stand idly by' as Democrats take control of Congress
articles.summary: In the face of an electoral rout, Senate Majority Leader John Thune declared that Senate Republicans will work with President Donald Trump against "Democrat...
articles.body:
In the face of an electoral rout, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said that Republicans in the upper congressional chamber will work with President Donald Trump to block "Democrat extremism."

Democrats delivered a drubbing, flipping control of both chambers of Congress, which means that the GOP will be relegated to the minority in both the House and Senate when the 120th Congress begins early next year.

Thune said that the Senate GOP has notched significant achievements and will not stand aside as the left seeks to uproot their work.

"Over the last two years, Senate Republicans have put up a strong record of accomplishment that's created safer streets, more money in Americans' pockets, and new opportunities for families and businesses to get ahead," Thune said in a post on X.

"After fighting Democrat obstruction at every turn, we prevented the largest tax hike in American history, secured our border in an unprecedented way, confirmed the president's Cabinet at the fastest pace in two decades, and put strong conservative judges on benches across the country faster than we have since the Reagan administration," Thune continued. "I'm proud of our team and everything we've done for the American people, and I'm looking forward to the important work we have in front of us over the next few months.

"As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we've done. Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we'll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism. We cannot let their fringe positions become the mainstream," the lawmaker concluded.

While the outcomes of tight Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska remain unclear, so far, the available election results indicate that Republicans will only have 44 Senate seats in the next Congress.

articles.title: TV Ratings: Blue Wave Fuels Surge in Midterm Election Night Viewing, NBC Leads Primetime
articles.summary: If the numbers hold, NBC will be the first broadcast network to win an election night in total viewers since 2012.
articles.body:
A dominant showing by Democrats in the 2026 midterms also resulted in — at least for one night — a realignment in viewing of election night news coverage.

Early data from Nielsen shows NBC leading primetime Tuesday night, by a wide enough margin that it will likely hold up through further adjustments to the ratings. That's a big change from the 2022 midterms, when NBC finished fourth among the six most watched news outlets. NBC also claimed the most watched live stream of election night with its "Kornacki Cam," focused solely on data analyst and video board operator Steve Kornacki.

In the likely event the preliminary ratings carry through, NBC will be the first broadcast network to lead a federal election night in total viewers since the 2012 presidential election (also topped by NBC). Election coverage across outlets is already up compared to 2022, but it might not hit the historically high levels of the 2018 midterms .

NBC averaged 6.8 million viewers in primetime, based on Nielsen fast national ratings, including out of home viewing. ABC finished second with 5.12 million viewers. The three largest cable news channels — CNN (4.159 million), MS NOW (4.156 million) and Fox News (4.04 million) — are currently within 120,000 viewers of one another. CBS is further back at 2.73 million viewers.

The fast nationals don't include Nielsen's big data component, so the numbers are pretty likely to change some. NBC should hold onto its primetime lead, but the cable networks are so tightly bunched that the order could easily get mixed up. This story will be updated, including comparisons to networks' performance four years ago, as more ratings data becomes available.

The combined total of 27.05 million viewers across the six networks is already ahead of the final, 12-network total for the 2022 midterms of 25.43 million . The 2018 total of 36.11 million viewers across 11 outlets, the highest for a midterm election night this century, is probably out of reach.

NBC also had a sizable lead in the core TV news ad demographic of adults 25-54, averaging 2.93 million in primetime. ABC (1.71 million) and CNN (1.55 million) followed, while Fox News (800,000), CBS (771,000) and MS NOW (764,000) were tightly bunched. Fox Business, which simulcast the Fox News feed, drew 323,000 viewers and 77,000 adults 25-54.

The live stream of the Kornacki Cam generated 29 million views across all platforms, NBC News says, including 6.1 million on YouTube. It peaked there with some 300,000 concurrent streams between 8:30 and 11:30 p.m. ET.

articles.summary: Conservative commentator Scott Jennings on Tuesday called the GOP’s losses in the 2026 midterms a “country a‑‑ whooping.” “Well, look, I’m not going to sugar...
articles.body:
Conservative commentator Scott Jennings on Tuesday called the GOP's losses in the 2026 midterms a "country a‑‑ whooping."

"Well, look, I'm not going to sugarcoat it. There's a political science term for what's happening. It's called a country a‑‑ whooping. That's what's happening right now, across the board," Jennings said on CNN Tuesday night.

"Look, you know, there's a lot of reasons for what's happening right now. The most immediate issue is cost of living and gas prices, and that is the bottom line," he added. "You could read into a lot of other things. You can be jubilant about this, that, or the other. But at the end of the day, the American people have here and now concerns, and that's really the lesson you got to take away from this."

Democrats locked down both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, most likely stymieing President Trump's policy agenda for the next two years.

Republicans faced an uphill battle this election cycle amid Trump's slumping approval rating, the unpopularity of the war in Iran and cost-of-living concerns.

According to a polling average from The Hill's partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Trump's approval rating was sitting at 38.4 percent Wednesday evening, with his disapproval rating at 58.7 percent.

Democrats are projected to go from 47 seats in their Senate caucus to 55, according to DDHQ , and from 214 seats in the House to 261. They also notched victories in states like Texas and Kansas, which have historically leaned red.

articles.title: Mississippi Senate race heads to an extended vote count and possible ballot battle
articles.summary: The Mississippi Senate race may take days to resolve, as Democrat Scott Colom leads GOP Sen.
articles.body:
The Mississippi Senate race may take days to resolve, as Democrat Scott Colom leads GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 65 votes in the current vote count.

And as votes continue to be counted, all eyes are on an unknown number of ballots that could shift the result — and lead to a very murky recount process.

Mississippi has not been a site of close vote counts and postelection drama in recent years. But Colom's strong showing comes as Democrats swept several Senate races in red states across the country. While Democrats will have a Senate majority without flipping Mississippi, it could be their reddest pickup.

And it would be another victory in a string of wins in the South, including in Texas and South Carolina, after years of struggle for Democrats.

National operatives are descending on the state, with staff members from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and the Elias Law Group on the ground Wednesday to lead the Democratic effort to ensure votes are counted, according to a source familiar with the effort, who was granted anonymity to discuss legal strategy.

A partner with the Elias Law Group, which has served as the Colom campaign's lawyers, told NBC News they were heading to Mississippi to investigate the outstanding vote.

Colom, a local prosecutor, said at a news conference Wednesday morning: "We're prepared to litigate, though we were prepared for this for months. We have an army of lawyers. We have local lawyers. We have everybody involved to make sure the process is followed according to the law."

Colom and Hyde-Smith's campaign manager , Jake Monssen , both said Wednesday that there are "thousands" of outstanding ballots. But the exact number remains unclear.

Around 6,000 mail ballots appear to have been distributed but not yet been returned Monday, according to data from the Mississippi secretary of state's office, which did not reply to a request for comment. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day can be counted in Mississippi if they are received by 5 p.m. Nov. 10.

An unknown number of so-called affidavit ballots, also known as provisional ballots, are also outstanding. Those were issued to voters who do not have the proper ID or are not on the list of registered voters.

Mikell Bolden, the Mississippi Democratic Party's executive director, said in a phone interview Wednesday that the party's election hotline received around 2,000 calls Tuesday from across the state, many of them from voters who were told they had to cast affidavit ballots.

Voters said they were certain they were registered to vote, Bolden said, but were told they were not on the voter roll when they went to cast their ballots. And Bolden said those voters could not check their own registration status, because the secretary of state's website had crashed.

Bolden said the state party, the Colom campaign and the national party are working to reach out to voters via phone calls, text messages and robocalls to ensure those who were affected return their ballots or address issues related to their affidavit ballots, like showing the proper ID, by Tuesday, which would allow them to be counted.

"Everything is on the line right now for this state," Bolden said.

And it will be a weeklong scramble — county election officials must transmit the election results to the secretary of state by Nov. 13.

Republicans are also signaling that they are gearing up for a legal fight.

Hyde-Smith campaign manager Jake Monssen said in a statement Wednesday that the campaign is "closely monitoring the remaining count" and is confident she will prevail.

Joanna Rodriguez, a National Republican Senatorial Committee spokeswoman, told NBC News in a statement, "As the democratic process continues to play out, we are committed to ensuring that every single lawful ballot is accurately counted and the voice of all Mississippians is heard."

While the focus is on the outstanding ballots, there are also new questions about a potential recount.

Ben Griffith, a voting rights and election law attorney who teaches at the University of Mississippi, told NBC News the options for Colom or Hyde-Smith to challenge the results are limited.

There is no mechanism for an election to undergo a recount under Mississippi state law. There is also no mechanism for a U.S. Senate general election race to be otherwise contested, according to state law and the Mississippi election handbook .

Candidates can challenge the results county by county by filing their intentions with particular county clerks to "examine" the contents of the counties' ballot box. But with 82 counties across the state and nine days until the canvassing must be complete, "that's beyond the scope of feasibility," Griffith said.

There are avenues for candidates in local elections across the state to challenge results of particular races with the Legislature — but not the U.S. Senate race.

articles.title: Iran takes credit for handing Trump a midterm defeat
articles.summary: Republicans’ resounding midterms defeat prompted quiet jubilation in Europe and exultation in Iran.
articles.body:
Republicans' resounding defeat Tuesday prompted quiet jubilation in Europe and exultation in Iran, as foreign capitals sized up a domestically constrained White House.

Tehran took credit for handing US President Donald Trump "a strategic defeat on the battlefield… and a POLITICAL DEFEAT in Washington ," following reports that Iranian negotiators stalled talks to keep US gas prices high.

Washington's European allies, who have navigated two years of friction with the US over military funding, the Ukraine war , and Greenland, were largely silent, though Italy's former prime minister said "Europe is much stronger" thanks to the "blue wave." Others were less sanguine. Trump is "quite weakened," France's economy minister acknowledged, but noted that the "unpredictable" president remains " in charge of international policy ."

articles.title: Trump approval rating sank as gas prices rose heading into midterms
articles.summary: Following a bad midterms for Republicans, here's how Trump's sinking approval rating correlated with rising gas prices so far this year.
articles.body:
For many voters, dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress' handling of the cost of living and gas prices in the United States fueled a historic night for Democrats in the Nov. 3 midterms.

That deep discontent over gas prices, specifically, has contributed to Trump's unpopularity , with his net approval rating down almost 20 percentage points since the beginning of the year.

On Election Day, the average price of gas in the United States was $4.14, according to AAA . That number was higher than the average in the first week of November in any election year since 1994, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) data.

"New election day record: the highest ever national average for gasoline and diesel prices ever on election day," Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in an X post on Election Day.

According to an Oct. 8 poll from Navigator Research , 76% of registered U.S. voters disapproved of Trump's handling of gas prices, while only 20% approved. The poll also showed that 73% of registered voters disapproved of Trump's handling of inflation and the cost of living, while just 23% approved.

"President Trump's approval ratings have hit all-time lows in Navigator tracking," the pollster said. "Majorities disapprove of Trump's handling of gas prices, inflation and the cost of living, and foreign policy."

In a USA TODAY analysis of average monthly gas prices from the EIA and net approval ratings from Reuters/Ipsos , Trump's continuous slide in the polls coincides with surging fuel costs.

Gas prices began to surge soon after the war on Iran began back in late February. Now, more than eight months since the start of the conflict, Trump recognized the role the war had in Republicans' bad night.

"I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term," Trump said about the war on Nov. 4, with Vice President JD Vance echoing a similar sentiment following the GOP's losses.

"At the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again because long term, it's the only answer," Trump continued. "You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon."

USA TODAY's Francesca Chambers and Keith Laing contributed to this report.

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

articles.title: Don Jr. Gets Relentlessly Booed on Celebratory Outing
articles.summary: Donald Trump Jr. was met with a barrage of boos and heckles during a visit to a law school in the aftermath of Republicans suffering a midterm drubbing. Stud...
articles.body:
Donald Trump Jr. was met with a barrage of boos and heckles during a visit to a law school in the aftermath of Republicans suffering a midterm drubbing.

Students at Emory University School of Law in Atlanta made their displeasure clear when the 48-year-old showed up on campus on Wednesday.

"The country has rebuked you guys! The country has rebuked you," one person yelled as Don Jr. made his way through one of the buildings, according to a video published by TMZ .

Other students erupted in boos and jeers before one heckler twists the knife, shouting, "We have the House and the Senate!"

A Secret Service agent appears to motion for the crowd to quiet down, to no avail.

Don Jr. was at Emory to support his business partner, Omeed Malik, whose name was being added to a building at his alma mater in a ribbon-cutting ceremony, TMZ reports, citing an unnamed source.

The visit reportedly surprised students, who were not told beforehand that Don Jr. would be attending.

Emory Law School did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Malik, who is seen in the video giving the students the middle finger, is the co-founder and president of 1789 Capital, a venture capital firm where Don Jr. is a partner.

The company's explosive growth since Don Jr. came aboard after his father won the presidency in 2024 has drawn intense scrutiny.

Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee have opened an investigation into the firm, accusing it of "insider political influence and thoroughgoing corruption"—allegations the company has denied.

Don Jr. was left licking his wounds on Election Day after his desperate election-eve blitz through Ohio and New York fell flat.

During one campaign event in Swanton, Ohio, on Monday, Don Jr. mistakenly claimed Democratic candidates "want to make Ohio a state."

Voters ultimately ousted Republican Sen. Jon Husted and rejected gubernatorial hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy.

In New York, Don Jr. stumped for GOP House candidate Kailee Buller, who lost her bid to unseat Democratic Rep. John Mannion.

Don Jr. subsequently threw his full support behind JD Vance's election postmortem, which amounted to a thinly veiled swipe at President Donald Trump's biggest priorities.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote, while singling out rising gas prices and the cost of living.

Barely an hour later, Don Jr. reposted the vice president's postmortem, writing, "Every word of this is 💯💯💯."

articles.title: Idaho voters focused on the real issues during midterms, like choosing the Winchester 1873 as their state gun
articles.summary: Idaho voters chose the Winchester Model 1873 as the official state gun, making it one of 11 U.S. states with an official firearm designation.
articles.body:
Tuesday's midterm elections were a bit of a bloodbath for the Republican Party.

If you're a conservative, chances are you are looking for any silver lining to cope with the fact that Democrats took the GOP behind the woodshed last night.

I'm here to tell you it wasn't all bad, though, as states like Tennessee and Florida are still looking pretty red, so there's no need to get too down in the dumps.

One state that certainly has voters with their priorities straight is Idaho, and I'm not just saying that because their state GOP incumbents completed a clean sweep at the polls.

It seems the voters all throughout The Gem State were focused on the real issues that have been at the top of everyone's mind.

Not healthcare or grocery prices, but rather which firearm would become the official state gun of Idaho.

Six different firearms were presented on the ballot, presenting quite a grab bag of options, from a Colt .45 to an M1 Garand.

The Winchester Model 1873, aka "The Gun that Won the West," is now the official state gun of Idaho.

Man, what a crushing blow for the "Peacemaker," I was sure he was going to pull away late.

In all seriousness, that's a pretty cool thing to say.

Some states have an official marine mammal or dessert, but Idaho has a state gun.

It's actually not uncommon, either, as 11 U.S. states now have an official firearm.

Most of the states on the list are pretty predictable, including Texas and West Virginia. I was surprised to see Pennsylvania included, though, while my beloved Sunshine State is nowhere to be found.

Regardless, whenever your conservative buddies get a little down in the dumps this week, just remind them that Idaho now has a state gun.

That'll go a long way in "owning the libs!"

articles.title: Blue wave crashes into data centers
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Data centers lose big during midterm races Fierce pushback to data centers helped carry Democrats to victory in key races across the nation this week, and where the centers were explicitly on the ballot, they lost overwhelmingly. © Greg Nash Midterm voters both rejected…
articles.body:
Data centers lose big during midterm races

Fierce pushback to data centers helped carry Democrats to victory in key races across the nation this week, and where the centers were explicitly on the ballot, they lost overwhelmingly .

Midterm voters both rejected industry-backed candidates and overwhelmingly backed resolutions to halt data center construction , dealing a major blow to the sector.

Election Day marked perhaps the biggest test so far for data center sentiment. Technology watchdog groups are seizing on the outcome, stating results show the public is largely rejecting the facilities and the technology they power.

“Data centers represent a fear and an angst that voters have about being replaced by AI, losing their jobs, losing their livelihoods [and] the rising price of energy in their local area,” said Brendan Steinhauser, who ran Sen. John Cornyn’s (R-Texas) 2014 campaign and is now CEO of the Alliance for Secure AI. He added that they were also representative of “corruption” from “Big Tech oligarchs.”

While the economy, high costs at the pump , corruption and the state of democracy topped voters’ list of concerns , exit polls suggest data centers were one of several factors contributing to the blue tsunami Tuesday night.

In an NBC News exit poll , 23 percent of voters said that data centers were “crucial” in their congressional vote, while another 33 percent said they were a “major” factor. Seventy-six percent said they would oppose construction of a new data center in their community.

“This is an issue that really defined affordability for folks, and governors, senators, House-elect members all saw it as a huge opportunity,” Lori Lodes, president of Climate Power, told reporters.

articles.summary: DSA co-chair Megan Romer dismissed the White House's $49 trillion price tag for socialist policies as a "made-up number" and declined to offer her own.
articles.body: Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) national co-chair Megan Romer was pressed on Fox News about how much socialist policies will cost American taxpayers after DSA-backed candidates made significant gains in midterm elections. The White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) estimated that DSA policy proposals, including Medicare for All and student debt cancellation, would cost taxpayers $49 trillion. Romer, who said the group's incoming lawmakers will prioritize affordability, dismissed the staggering price tag as "outrageous," calling it a "made-up number." "The White House, who does not like us very much, managed to come up with some math that made us look bad," Romer said on "The Story." "But we don't agree with these numbers." RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY The CEA’s report estimated the DSA’s policy wish list will cost about $355,000 per American household over the next decade. After rejecting the administration's figures, Romer declined to offer an independent estimate of her own when pressed by Fox News anchor Martha MacCallum, saying the cost "depends." DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT "There's no, like, one, solid number because it depends on what pieces we can build in the meantime," the DSA leader said. "So it's about building up programs and then sunsetting old, bad programs, and that number is going to shift as we pass various things." "I'm not going to give you a solid number. That's not what I'm here to do," she continued. "What I'm here to do is talk about how we collectively can democratically decide how we want our money to be spent." SOCIALIST PRIMARY SWEEP SPARKS LAUNCH OF NEW RESOURCE LAYING OUT WHAT’S AT STAKE IN 2026 Romer criticized the scale of U.S. military spending, arguing that federal resources devoted to overseas military operations would be better redirected toward the DSA's policy priorities, including amnesty for illegal immigrants and abolishing the Senate. "We don't believe in having 800 U.S. military bases around the world," Romer said. "That is an insane amount of money to spend… Our military spending is outrageous, and most of that money is going to defense contractors. It is making a handful of billionaires richer." SEN DEB FISCHER: THE LEFT'S WAR ON THE SENATE AND SUPREME COURT PUTS OUR REPUBLIC AT RISK MacCallum countered her claims about excessive military spending, saying the U.S. defense budget is only $961 billion compared to an estimated $47 trillion for DSA policies to be funded. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In a July interview with Fox News, Romer stood by her positions to abolish the Senate, replace the presidency and Supreme Court, and to eradicate Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She also defended wanting to abolish borders and grant amnesty to illegal immigrants in the United States. "We do agree that it will cost money to provide healthcare to everyone, but it will cost less money than we spend on the military and on these illegal wars right now," Romer said Wednesday.

articles.title: Felipe Sousa-Lazaballet: as propostas do brasileiro eleito na Flórida | G1
articles.standfirst: Nascido no Rio de Janeiro e criado em Santa Cruz da Serra, em Duque de Caxias, Felipe Sousa-Lazaballet, de 40 anos, será o primeiro brasileiro a ocupar uma cadeira na Assembleia Legislativa da Flórida
articles.summary: Felipe Sousa-Lazaballet, carioca de 40 anos, assume vaga histórica na Flórida com foco em reduzir custos de moradia e ampliar o acesso à saúde no estado americano.
articles.body:
O brasileiro Felipe Sousa-Lazaballet, de 40 anos, foi eleito deputado estadual na Flórida , nos Estados Unidos, pelo Partido Democrata. Nascido na cidade do Rio de Janeiro e criado em Santa Cruz da Serra, em Duque de Caxias, na Baixada Fluminense, ele será o primeiro brasileiro a ocupar uma cadeira na Assembleia Legislativa do estado.

Entre as principais propostas que pretende defender durante o mandato estão a ampliação do acesso à saúde pública, o aumento dos investimentos em educação e medidas para reduzir os custos da moradia.

Antes de entrar na política, Felipe atuava como diretor-executivo de uma organização não governamental (ONG) que atende cerca de 35 mil imigrantes. A decisão de disputar uma eleição veio após a reeleição de Donald Trump à Presidência dos Estados Unidos.

Segundo o brasileiro, duas semanas depois do resultado, ele recebeu uma ligação de uma deputada estadual que ocupava a cadeira e o incentivou a disputar o cargo.

"Eu lembro que naquele dia da eleição eu sentei no meu carro e pensei: nossa, a gente vai viver nesse mundo agora com governadores que são super anti-imigrantes."

A campanha durou quase dois anos. Durante a disputa, a equipe visitou cerca de 42 mil residências e fez contato telefônico com 20 mil pessoas no último fim de semana antes da votação. O objetivo era apresentar as propostas e incentivar os eleitores a comparecer às urnas.

"Chegamos a tocar 42 mil portas, ou seja, porta a porta. Ligamos a 20 mil pessoas no último fim de semana para poder falar com as pessoas, incentivar elas a saírem e a votar, contar para elas da importância do voto", afirmou.

Moradia, saúde e educação entre as prioridades

Felipe Sousa-Lazaballet — Foto: Divulgação

A plataforma de campanha de Felipe, chamada "Prosperando Juntos", reúne propostas em quatro áreas: habitação, educação pública, saúde e meio ambiente.

Na área habitacional, ele defende medidas de proteção para pessoas que vivem de aluguel e a ampliação de fundos destinados à construção de moradias com preços acessíveis. O deputado eleito também pretende discutir o custo dos seguros residenciais na Flórida.

"Segundo ele, a expansão poderia ampliar o acesso aos serviços de saúde para um contingente entre 800 mil e 1,4 milhão de pessoas na Flórida."

Segundo Felipe, os valores elevados dos seguros encarecem os financiamentos imobiliários e dificultam o acesso à casa própria.

"As pessoas na Flórida pagam o maior índice desses seguros, que fazem com que a hipoteca fique cada vez mais cara. Isso significa que fica mais difícil as pessoas conseguirem um dia ter uma casa própria", afirmou.

Na educação, as propostas incluem o aumento dos investimentos nas escolas públicas e dos salários dos professores.

Já na saúde, Felipe defende a ampliação do Medicaid, programa de assistência médica financiado pelos governos federal e estaduais. Segundo ele, a expansão poderia ampliar o acesso aos serviços de saúde para um contingente entre 800 mil e 1,4 milhão de pessoas na Flórida.

A proteção ambiental e a defesa dos direitos civis também estão entre as prioridades anunciadas pelo deputado eleito.

Felipe Sousa-Lazaballet nos Estados Unidos — Foto: Acervo pessoal

Felipe reconhece que terá desafios para colocar em prática as propostas, já que o Partido Democrata continuará sendo minoria na Assembleia Legislativa da Flórida.

Apesar disso, ele citou mudanças na composição do Legislativo estadual após as eleições. Segundo o brasileiro, os democratas conquistaram 16 cadeiras que antes eram ocupadas por republicanos.

"Estou indo com essa pauta progressista para a capital do estado aqui na Flórida e vou fazer o máximo para poder conseguir alcançá-las ou chegar perto daquilo", afirmou.

articles.title: STM: Perda de patente de Bolsonaro deve ser julgada só em 2027 | G1
articles.standfirst: Caso tramita desde fevereiro no STM, que julga crimes militares de competência federal. Aprovação de uma anistia a Bolsonaro pelo Congresso pode esvaziar análise sobre a punição.
articles.summary: O STM deve adiar para 2027 o julgamento sobre a perda de patente de Bolsonaro e generais, em meio a discussões sobre anistia para os envolvidos na trama golpista.
articles.body:
lO Superior Tribunal Militar (STM) deve deixar para 2027 os julgamentos dos pedidos de perda dos postos e das patentes do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), do ex-comandante da Marinha Almir Garnier e dos generais Augusto Heleno, Paulo Sérgio Nogueira e Walter Souza Braga Netto.

🔎 O STM é o órgão máximo da Justiça Militar da União no Brasil. É responsável por processar e julgar crimes militares definidos no Código Penal Militar, tanto em tempo de paz quanto em tempo de guerra.

A punição foi determinada pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) no julgamento que condenou, em setembro de 2025, Bolsonaro e aliados na trama golpista e pedida pelo Ministério Público Militar ao STM em fevereiro deste ano.

De lá pra cá, os processos pouco avançaram e a maioria está sem registro público de andamentos desde setembro.

O STM aponta que estão sendo cumpridas diligências determinadas pelos gabinetes responsáveis.

Enquanto não têm a perda da patente oficializada, os militares continuam recebendo do governo, mesmo estando na reserva. Em setembro, os valores pagos a eles foram:

No STM, esse tipo de ação leva, em média, de seis a 11 meses para ser julgada. Essa é a primeira vez que a Corte vai analisar um caso envolvendo crime contra a democracia.

Inicialmente, ministros do STM indicaram que os casos deveriam ser julgados após as eleições de outubro. A previsão não se confirmou e a sinalização é de que a análise das representações para Declaração de Indignidade para o Oficialato dos cinco militares só ocorra em 2027.

Além das etapas processuais alegadas pelo tribunal, o caso segue para a avaliação do ministro-revisor após o relator liberar seu voto. O prazo é considerado curto visto que o tribunal entrará em recesso em 20 de dezembro.

Outro argumento para cautela no julgamento é que há discussões no Congresso Nacional sobre uma possível articulação em torno de uma anistia para o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro , evitando que ele tenha que cumprir a pena de 27 anos e três meses de prisão. O que poderia impactar as ações no STM.

Se os relatores destravarem os casos, também não está descartado um pedido de vista, ou seja, mais prazo para o julgamento.

Nas carreiras militares, o posto é o grau hierárquico dos oficiais, como capitão e general, e representa o nível de autoridade que aquele militar ocupa na estrutura de comando. A patente é o documento que garante esse posto.

A Constituição Federal estabelece que a Justiça Militar deve julgar se um militar condenado a mais de dois anos de prisão de forma definitiva deve ser considerado indigno para o oficialato.

Na prática, a Justiça Militar precisa julgar se o militar tem condições de continuar na carreira ou se deve ser excluído das Forças Armadas.

Bolsonaro, que é capitão reformado, e os militares faziam parte do chamado núcleo crucial da trama golpista.

No caso de Bolsonaro, o STM chegou a negar em junho um pedido da defesa afastar o ministro Joseli Parente do processo após elogios ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) feito pelo magistrado, além de comentários sobre o julgamento dos militares à imprensa.

Os ministros consideraram o pedido insuficiente para sustentar uma parcialidade.

O STM é formado por 15 ministros – sendo 10 militares e 5 civis. A presidente do STM só vota em caso de empate. O regimento prevê que neste caso o voto é a favor do réu.

Uma decisão a favor do pedido do MP impacta a remuneração do militar, que deixa de receber salário, mas o familiar dependente (esposa, companheiras ou filhas) recebe uma pensão — é a chamada "morte ficta".

articles.summary: No Senado, o partido Democrata virou sete cadeiras e tem maioria garantida, com 54 de 100 senadores. Na Câmara, as projeções indicam mais de 250 cadeiras para os democratas.
articles.body:
Ainda na noite de terça-feira (3), o presidente americano disse à imprensa que aceita a derrota e que irá precisar negociar com os democratas. O resultado das urnas foi tão avassalador para o partido Republicano que não deixou margem para contestações. No Senado, o partido Democrata virou sete cadeiras e tem maioria garantida, com 54 de 100 senadores (e ainda pode conquistar mais duas posições; Alasca e Mississipi ainda apuram os votos). Na Câmara, a projeção do jornal The New York Times para o placar final aponta mais de 250 cadeiras para os democratas, mais do que o suficiente para alcançar a maioria, com 218 (atualmente, o partido tem 214 representantes). Os democratas elegeram também, pela primeira vez na história americana, uma governadora negra, uma senadora indígena, um senador abertamente gay e um senador muçulmano.

Neste episódio, Victor Boyadjian recebe dois convidados. Primeiro, ele fala com o jornalista Eduardo Graça, que, diretamente dos EUA, conta o que ouviu dos eleitores e revela o que apurou nos bastidores dos partidos Democrata e Republicano. Depois, Oliver Stuenkel analisa o que esperar dos próximos dois anos de governo Trump, inclusive na política externa e nas relações com o Brasil.

Convidados: Eduardo Graça, colunista e repórter do jornal O Globo e responsável pelo blog Trump 2.0, e Oliver Stuenkel, professor de Relações Internacionais da FGV e pesquisador do Carnegie Endowment.

O podcast O Assunto é produzido por: Luiz Felipe Silva, Carlos Catelan, Luiz Gabriel Franco, Juliene Moretti, Stéphanie Nascimento, Marco Antônio Martins e Thomé Granemann. Na apresentação: Natuza Nery.

O Assunto é o podcast diário produzido pelo g1, disponível em todas as plataformas de áudio e no YouTube. Desde a estreia, em agosto de 2019, o podcast O Assunto soma mais de 168 milhões de downloads em todas as plataformas de áudio.
