articles.title: 5 healthcare fights Democrats could take on after midterms sweep
articles.summary: Democrats will have leverage to try to restore the expired Obamacare tax credits, reverse Medicaid cuts and push for changes they say would make healthcare m...
articles.body:
Democrats' victories in the midterm elections could have a major impact on Americans' healthcare, from how much people pay for health insurance and prescription drugs to what coverage is available to them, according to health policy experts and former White House advisers. If the Democrats and President Donald Trump are willing to work together, that is.

With control of the House and Senate, Democrats will hold significant leverage to restore the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies , reverse cuts to Medicaid and push for changes they say would make healthcare more affordable.

They can also use their oversight powers to scrutinize the Trump administration's health policies, including those led by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The new Democratic majority will include three doctors who have been vocal in their criticism of the health secretary, including Sen.-elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, and Rep.-elect Richard Pan of California. During her campaign, Andrews criticized Kennedy for overhauling the federal vaccine schedule and promoting medical disinformation, calling him an "archnemesis" to public health.

"We've seen a real transformation of the healthcare state over the last two years and it's been immensely damaging," said Miranda Yaver, an assistant professor of health policy and management at the University of Pittsburgh. "We can absolutely expect to see a lot of oversight into these changes and unpacking what those harms are."

But turning those policies into law won't be easy. Any legislation would still need Trump's signature, setting up a potential clash over the future of healthcare. Ahead of Tuesday's election, Trump said he'd brand himself "Mr. Veto" if Democrats took control of Congress. On Wednesday, he said he'll "probably" get along with the Democrats.

"The way I think about this is hunting versus farming," said John Barkett, a former White House policy adviser under the Biden administration, where he covered drug pricing. "Next Congress, there's going to be a lot of farming. Hunting, you go for a big kill. If those pass, probably not going to happen [with Trump]. But can you sow seeds and prepare land for growth over time? Yes."

Here are five ways Democrats could take on healthcare.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has said restoring the expired enhanced ACA tax credits would be a primary objective for Democrats if they took control of Congress in 2027.

When those federal subsidies expired at the end of last year, millions saw their monthly premium bills double or even triple — forcing about 3 million people to walk away from their coverage altogether. Others switched to cheaper plans that offered worse coverage.

In 2027, costs are expected to rise even more. ACA premiums are jumping by double digits for the second year in a row, and a mix of lower enrollment and rising healthcare costs is driving some major insurers to pull out of the market .

Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group, said that if Democrats manage to negotiate a deal with Trump to restore the enhanced subsidies, the relief could be backdated to the beginning of 2027. That means anyone who paid the higher premiums would get that money back as a refund.

"That could both increase enrollment and provide cost relief to current ACA enrollees," he said.

Dr. Ezekiel Emanuel, a special adviser for health policy during the Obama administration, said he supports Democrats pursuing reimplementing ACA subsidies as long as they can find the money for it and they don't lose sight of rising insurance costs for other Americans.

"One of the dangers of big election victories is people get cocky and they overreach and they fail to deliver on what people actually care about," he said. "Half of all Americans get their insurance through employer-sponsored insurance."

The Medicaid cuts under Trump's "big, beautiful bill," especially the Medicaid work requirements, are also expected to draw significant pushback from Democrats.

The work requirements are expected to strip coverage from millions of people — not for lack of employment, but due to burdensome paperwork and other red tape. A number of states have already started implementing the requirements ahead of the national Jan. 1 deadline.

Last week, a federal judge in Boston dealt a blow to the administration's work rules , blocking a policy from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services that would have forced "medically frail" patients and people with disabilities to prove they are too "significantly impaired" to adhere to the new work mandates. The judge also granted states an additional six months to implement the more lenient version.

Levitt said Trump is bound to veto any bills rolling back Medicaid cuts.

"Then the game of chess between Democrats and Trump will begin to figure out what healthcare can actually get enacted," Levitt said.

It's also possible a number of states could finally expand Medicaid. Ten states have not adopted the full Medicaid expansion under the ACA. That includes Georgia, Texas and Wisconsin, which elected Democratic governors on Tuesday, alongside Kansas, where the race remains too close to call.

Yaver was skeptical, noting that Trump's "big, beautiful bill" ended financial incentives that encouraged states to adopt the expansion.

"I think we're absolutely going to see efforts to increase Medicaid access," she said. "I just don't know what Medicaid expansion looks like without the increased financial incentive."

Democrats could find common ground with Trump on efforts to lower healthcare costs, particularly prescription drug prices, Emanuel said.

Trump has made lowering drug costs a priority during his second term, through his discount prescription drug website TrumpRx and his "most favored nation" drug pricing deals. Democrats could push to build on those efforts, while pursuing other changes they say would make drugs more affordable.

"I think there is probably a very big agreement you could reach with him," Emanuel said.

But Democrats may not find the dealmaker they want in Trump, Barkett said.

"Remember, the big thing Trump has done on drug prices is sign these deals that no one has seen with drug manufacturers, and it's not even clear the drug manufacturers were hurt by those deals," Barkett said.

Yaver said another way Democrats could work with Trump is through legislation limiting the use of prior authorization, a cost-cutting tool insurers use that requires patients to get approval before receiving certain treatments. The tool has been blamed by doctors and patients for delaying necessary care. The Trump administration has already made moves to crack down on the practice.

"That is generating not just bipartisan support but unanimous support at the state level," she said.

There could also be a bipartisan pushback on the rising cost of hospital care as well as pharmacy benefit managers, which act as middlemen to negotiate drug prices and rebates on behalf of insurers and employers. The PBMs have faced criticisms after research has shown their practices can drive up the cost of healthcare.

With control of congressional committees, Democrats will have power to hold hearings, demand documents and subpoena administration officials to testify.

Emanuel said Kennedy is likely to face Democratic probes over his moves on vaccines, including overhauling the CDC's vaccine advisory panel, changing the federal vaccine schedule and taking steps to alter the federal Vaccine Injury Compensation Program .

The health secretary has also faced widespread criticism and blame for the resurgence of measles in the U.S. This year, there have been more than 4,850 measles cases , the highest number in at least 30 years.

"Some of that does need to happen because that has to stop," Emanuel said.

Barkett said the investigations might play to the Democrats' advantage by distracting the Trump administration and potentially freezing any new policies.

"It takes up their time," he said. "And everything they encounter, whatever they uncover, could be more campaign fodder [for 2028]."

"Medicare for All" will remain a central goal for many Democrats, even if the proposal is unlikely to become law under a Republican president.

The most popular version of the proposal would establish a government-run health insurance program covering all Americans.

"I'm not a big advocate of 'Medicare for All,' but at the moment, the only plan out there is 'Medicare for All,'" Emanuel said. "We need to have more plans, and we have between now and the start of 2028 to have plans."

Still, introducing a "Medicare for All" bill and pushing for a vote could give supporters a chance to make their case and build momentum for a broader overhaul of the healthcare system if Democrats win the White House in 2028.

That falls under "the more symbolic category, because as we know, Donald Trump is going to veto big progressive actions," Yaver said.

articles.title: 5 takeaways on the demographic shifts that powered the Democrats’ midterm victory
articles.summary: The dust has not yet settled from the seismic midterm elections, but the contours of the Democratic triumph are becoming clearer. Several key demographic groups have moved toward Democrats since President Trump defeated then-Vice President Kamala Harris two years ago. In aggregate, these shifts powered a massive repudiation of Trump and the GOP. As of…
articles.body:
The dust has not yet settled from the seismic midterm elections, but the contours of the Democratic triumph are becoming clearer.

Several key demographic groups have moved toward Democrats since President Trump defeated then-Vice President Kamala Harris two years ago. In aggregate, these shifts powered a massive repudiation of Trump and the GOP.

As of Wednesday evening, Democrats had won at least 54 Senate seats, while The Hill’s data and polling partner Decision Desk HQ is projecting the party will end up with 261 House seats. This would put the Democrats above their high-water mark of the Obama years, 257.

A more granular look at the election is possible because of two major studies.

One is the “ voter trends ” survey conducted by The New York Times, and the other is the voter poll commissioned by seven other major news organizations and carried out by SSRS. More details are publicly available on the methodology in both instances , which the organizations believe make these surveys more reliable than traditional exit polls.

The data may be refined over time, and these samples by their nature have some degree of imprecision or statistical “noise.” But the statistics are extensive enough to identify some of the most important trends.

Hispanic voters shifted sharply away from the GOP

Trump and his allies had taken pride in his previous showing with Hispanic voters, particularly since they felt it rebutted criticism that the president’s rhetoric on immigration doomed him with this group.

In 2024, the Times voter survey showed Trump winning 44 percent of Latino voters against Harris, while exit polls put him a notch higher at 46 percent. Either way, this represented the best performance of a GOP presidential nominee with Latino voters since at least 2004, when then-President George W. Bush won a second term.

It was a very different story Tuesday. The New York Times survey showed the GOP winning just 30 percent of Hispanic voters, while the SSRS voter poll put the number at 34 percent.

The fall-off will not have been caused by a single factor, and pre-election opinion polling suggested economic dissatisfaction across the whole electorate was a big drag on the GOP.

But it stands to reason that controversial immigration enforcement actions taken during the current administration will have hurt Republicans among Latino voters.

The New York Times reported last month that at least 25 people have been shot at by federal immigration officers during Trump’s second term, with six having been killed.

The SSRS voter poll included a question about public approval of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), though the available data does not break down those responses by race.

The poll showed a striking 50 percent of all voters saying they “strongly disapprove” of ICE’s performance and 94 percent of that cohort backing the Democrats.

Men moved against the GOP even more than women

The general shape of the gender divide in American politics has long been that women are more likely to vote Democratic and men more likely to vote Republican.

In 2024, in the Times voter survey, women backed Harris by 10 points over Trump while men favored him by 15 points.

The overall electorate moved sharply toward the Democrats on Tuesday but, strikingly, the shift was somewhat more pronounced among men than women.

Men overall actually broke for the Democrats, albeit by a modest 3 points in the Times survey and 2 points in SSRS. Still, the Times data indicated an 18-point swing toward Democrats among men, whereas the equivalent shift among women was just 13 points.

Interestingly, the pattern seemed to hold across racial groups. In the Times’s data, white men moved 15 points toward Democrats, against 11 points for their female counterparts, while non-white men shifted by 23 points and non-white women by only 16 points.

It could be merely that the GOP had more ground to lose with men, as it is otherwise difficult to deduce exactly which issues would have caused male support to erode to a greater extent than among women.

Young people shift strongly back to Democrats

Two years ago, when Trump won reelection, his performance among young voters caused delight among conservatives and made liberals fret.

Trump won 43 or 44 percent of voters under the age of 30, depending on the survey. This was, again, the highest share of the vote for a Republican presidential nominee since at least Bush in 2004.

After the 2024 election, there was a lot of media focus on the movement of young men toward the GOP — a shift that launched numerous think pieces about the influence of the “manosphere” and of podcasters with a particular appeal to young men, most famously Joe Rogan.

But Tuesday’s results suggested the GOP boom with young people is over — at least for now.

In the SSRS poll, the GOP won just 21 percent of voters under the age of 25, and 28 percent of those aged 25-29. The New York Times survey pegged Republican support among voters under 30 at 28 percent.

The Iran war could have had an influence here. Some of the commentators and influencers who are considered important with the younger demographic have been critical of Trump’s decision to join Israel in that conflict. In July, Rogan complained, “This war is not something anybody that’s conservative wanted.”

But dissatisfaction with the economy is surely playing on younger people’s minds too.

One thing is for sure, the purported “vibe shift” among younger voters toward the GOP appears to have been reversed.

GOP’s previous advances with Black voters also stall

It wasn’t only young voters who returned to their traditional pattern of favoring Democrats by big margins.

The SSRS voter poll showed Black voters going for Democrats by an 81-point margin, 90 points to 9 points. The New York Times survey showed a similar pattern, with Democrats prevailing 91-8.

Those statistics indicate a meaningful drop from the 2024 Times survey, which showed 13 percent of Black voters backing Trump — and from the exit polls from the 2022 midterms, which also pointed to 13 percent support for the GOP among African American voters.

Relatedly, significant media coverage of the marquee Senate race in Michigan had focused on whether Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed was struggling with Black voters. In the end, El-Sayed won his race comfortably, suggesting those concerns may have been exaggerated.

GOP shows more resilience among non-college whites

Republicans suffered such a rout Tuesday that they are searching for data that is less bad, in terms of the trends, rather than objectively good.

One example may come in the shape of a core MAGA constituency, white voters without a college education — especially men.

Although there has been some erosion with this bloc, it remains very strongly in the Republican camp.

The SSRS survey suggested white men without a college education went for the GOP on Tuesday by almost 30 points, 63-35. Their female counterparts favored Republicans by 16 points, 57-41.

The publicly available Times data did not break down this group by gender, but it did show non-college white voters continuing to back the GOP by 19 points, 59-40.

This isn’t exactly cause for celebration for Republicans — the Times survey noted this group still swung toward Democrat by 14 points since Trump’s 2024 win. But it does least remain solidly in the red corner overall.

articles.title: Democrats won Congress. But can they deliver on their promises?
articles.summary: Despite their midterm election victories, Democrats face major obstacles to reining in Trump on Iran, tariffs and more.
articles.body:
Democrats rode a blue wave to victory in the United States midterm elections , winning control of both chambers of Congress . Now comes the question of whether they can deliver on their promises.

The party campaigned on bringing down the cost of living, ending the war on Iran and holding President Donald Trump accountable, as well as pushing back against his immigration crackdown.

But Democrats won’t take control of Congress until January. Even then, there’s only so much they’ll be able to do without Republican cooperation.

Most bills need 60 votes to get past a filibuster in the Senate, and even if Democrats manage that, Trump can still veto their legislation. He has already threatened to do just that, telling a podcast on Monday, “I’ll veto everything.”

But the Democrats now also have other tools at their disposal, including power over Senate confirmations and control over committees that can launch investigations.

So what can Democrats realistically accomplish over the next two years, and where might they struggle to make good on their promises?

Can Democrats bring down the cost of living?

Affordability was one of the biggest issues for voters heading into Tuesday’s midterm elections, and Democrats seized on that, promising to bring down the costs of energy, housing, healthcare and groceries.

Dean Baker, an economist and cofounder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a US-based think tank, said one of the most effective things Democrats can do to bring down costs is push for an end to the war on Iran.

Since February, the conflict has driven up energy prices, as Iran has restricted commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for the oil and gas trade.

Baker argued that Democrats could use congressional investigations and oversight to pressure the Trump administration to end the war, potentially helping to give consumers relief.

Foreign policy is an area where some Republicans could find common cause with Democrats, said Baker.

Another area, he added, might be healthcare, an issue that similarly hits voters in the pocketbook.

The expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies in 2025 has left many Americans facing higher insurance premiums.

With their new congressional majorities, Democrats could push to restore those subsidies and reverse cuts to Medicaid, the government healthcare programme for low-income Americans.

A possible path to accomplishing that goal would be to include those measures in government spending bills that Congress needs to pass, according to Baker. That would also make them harder for Trump to reject.

“Republicans living in a post-Trump world, I don’t think they want to be on the side of preventing people from getting healthcare or basically paying more for healthcare,” Baker said. “They can make the politics such that he doesn’t want to veto it.”

Trump’s tariff campaign is another factor driving up consumer costs. But Baker warned that they could be tougher to reverse, without substantial support from Republicans to override a Trump veto. Even if they do manage that, prices could take a while to actually drop.

“Prices are like rockets and feathers. They shoot up like rockets; they come down like feathers,” said Alex Jacquez, chief of policy and advocacy at Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive economic think tank.

Jacquez, however, pointed to another path Democrats could take that wouldn’t need Trump’s approval.

With majorities in Congress, Democrats could wield congressional committees to investigate companies that have been raising the prices of everything from groceries to electricity bills.

“There’s a lot of precedent for getting some real material outcomes just through having the gavels and being able to subpoena CEOs and haul people in front of Congress,” Jacquez told Al Jazeera.

While there’s no guarantee these investigations would bring down prices, they could put pressure on companies to explain or adjust their decisions.

Could a Democratic Congress hold Trump accountable?

Laura Blessing, a senior fellow at Georgetown University’s Government Affairs Institute, expects Democrats to make extensive use of their new investigative powers.

“In terms of time spent and newspaper ink spilled, this is where you’re going to see the most action from Dems, by a mile,” she told Al Jazeera in an email.

Congressional investigations do not require White House approval. But they could make life harder for Trump by scrutinising his actions both within and outside of government.

Many Democrats have signalled they plan to investigate the source of the Trump family’s wealth as part of January’s incoming Congress.

Trump’s personal wealth has soared by about $2.2bn since the start of his term, according to financial disclosure forms released earlier this year.

His family’s business empire has likewise expanded over the last two years into everything from cryptocurrency and drones to artificial intelligence and prediction markets — industries his government has favoured in its policies.

Democratic senators have already been laying the groundwork for potential investigations, sending letters to companies and government departments demanding that they preserve records.

Among the issues they could examine are whether donors to Trump’s White House ballroom received favourable treatment from the government, and whether the Justice Department targeted his political opponents.

There is no guarantee, however, that everyone will cooperate.

Trump administration officials could challenge subpoenas in court, delaying investigations. But while Blessing doesn’t expect “Trump’s nuclear family to show up to a subpoena”, she said Democrats could still question government employees and others connected to Trump’s inner circle.

Even if they uncover wrongdoing, however, there is no guarantee of legal consequences, since it’s Trump’s own Justice Department that would have to decide whether to take up the cases.

Impeachment is another possibility. Lawmakers have already introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for multiple reasons, including allegations that he waged war against Iran without seeking congressional approval first.

Republican Representative Thomas Massie has said he will try to force a House vote on Hegseth’s impeachment when the outgoing Congress returns to session next week.

Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term, however, dismissed the prospect of facing a third impeachment himself, telling reporters on Wednesday that he was “not even a little bit” worried.

“I think it would destroy the Democratic Party if they did that, because it would be impeachment for no reason,” he said.

Trump also defended Hegseth, saying he was doing “a very good job”.

Even if the House of Representatives votes to impeach a government official, the case must still be weighed in a Senate trial.

Removing an elected official would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, meaning many Republicans would need to get on board to oust a figure like Trump or Hegseth. No president in US history has ever been removed from office as a result of an impeachment proceeding.

With less than two months until the 120th Congress is sworn in, experts anticipate Trump will use his final weeks with the outgoing Republican majorities to push through any remaining legislative priorities.

It also leaves Trump a critical window in which to escalate the war on Iran, according to Trita Parsi, the executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a foreign policy think tank.

“He has shown a pattern in which, in the face of humiliation and defeat, he becomes more reckless,” Parsi told Al Jazeera.

Democrats could pursue a binding resolution to wind down the war. After all, the US Constitution assigns Congress the sole authority to declare war, and laws like the War Powers Act of 1973 give lawmakers a path to ending unauthorised conflicts past the 60-day mark.

But there is no guarantee that those efforts would work, given the possibility of Trump vetoing their proposed measures.

Experts, however, say there is another way that Democrats could rein in Trump’s war powers. One of their most powerful tools will be control over government spending.

The Trump administration can continue using money already allocated for military operations, but Democrats could try to block additional funding for the war.

“It creates a limitation for how long he can pursue the war,” Parsi said. “If he needs more funding for it, we’re not talking about small sums that he can just reallocate from other places easily.”

With control of congressional committees, Democrats could also investigate the administration’s conduct during the war, including whether its military operations complied with US law.

“Rigorous oversight would not restrict military operations by itself but could raise the political costs of the war beyond what the president or other key officials are willing to endure,” said David Janovsky, a policy analyst at the Project on Government Oversight.

How much political will Democrats have to end the conflict, however, is an open question.

Blessing, the government affairs fellow, noted that the party has historically been reluctant to withhold military funding out of fear of being accused of undermining US troops.

But Parsi warned that failing to act would be politically unsustainable — and could be seen by the party’s base as a tacit endorsement of US military involvement in the Middle East.

“It will no longer be just Trump’s war,” Parsi said. “They will also co-own it, because they will be complicit, because they have the ability to stop it.”

Could Democrats rein in Trump’s immigration crackdown?

Another target for the incoming Democrat-led Congress could be Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown.

His pledge to oversee the largest mass deportation in US history has sparked widespread public backlash. A public opinion poll earlier this year found that 65 percent of Americans believe Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has “gone too far” in its efforts.

With control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats could launch investigations into ICE and other agencies involved in the crackdown.

Their probes could seek information about conditions inside detention centres, allegations of abuse and how taxpayer dollars are being used for immigration enforcement, said Heidi Altman, the vice president of policy at the National Immigration Law Center.

Altman argues Congress could also claw back the roughly $240bn already given to the Trump administration for immigration enforcement over the past two years.

That amount of money, she explained, has allowed ICE to operate with few constraints, without having to prioritise which communities to go into or who to detain.

“The only way to force a slowdown and actual sort of decision-making and prioritisation and enforcement is to dramatically curtail their budget by taking back the funding from the last session,” she said.

Doing so would require passing legislation that Trump could eventually veto. But Altman argued that Democrats should push ahead anyway.

“The worst possible thing we could do is throw up our hands and say we have limited power,” she said.

“Pass the bills, see what happens, put them on the president’s desk, and dare him to look at the American people and say he’s not signing something that they overwhelmingly demanded.”

articles.title: None of the House Republicans who voted to impeach Trump will be in the next Congress
articles.summary: None of the House Republicans who voted to impeach President Trump over the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol will be in Congress after this year, following Tuesday’s midterm elections. The last Republicans still in the House are outgoing Rep. David Valadao (Calif.), who was defeated by Democrat Randy Villegas on Tuesday, and Rep.…
articles.body:
None of the House Republicans who voted to impeach President Trump over the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol will be in Congress after this year, following Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The last Republicans still in the House are outgoing Rep. David Valadao (Calif.), who was defeated by Democrat Randy Villegas on Tuesday, and Rep. Dan Newhouse (Wash.), who is retiring.

Valadao and Newhouse were among the 10 House Republicans who crossed the aisle to impeach Trump following the Capitol attack. Former GOP Reps. Liz Cheney (Wyo.) and Adam Kinzinger (Ill.) were the only two to serve on the House Select Committee on Jan. 6, which infuriated Republicans and drew Trump’s ire.

In 2022, eight of the 10 either chose to not run for reelection or lost in the GOP primaries, including Cheney who lost to Trump-backed Rep. Harriet Hageman (R-Wyo.). At the time, Trump had endorsed a number of candidates in GOP primary battles in an effort to unseat Republicans who he believed crossed him following the 2020 election and Capitol attack.

Here’s a list of the 10 former House Republicans who voted to impeach Trump:

Cheney lost to Hageman in the primaries despite being a part of the Cheney political dynasty. She was a vocal critic of Trump and served as vice chair of the House Select Committee on Jan. 6.

Hageman recently ascended to Wyoming’s open Senate seat in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Cheney vowed she would do whatever she could to make sure Trump did not return anywhere near the White House after his first term.

The former Wyoming representative has since continued to advocate for traditional conservative causes while blasting Trump — even campaigning for former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race.

Former Rep. Anthony Gonzalez (Ohio) announced he would not be seeking another term in the House months after he voted to impeach Trump.

In the 2022 midterm elections, Trump instead endorsed Rep. Max Miller (R) in the race to lead Ohio’s 7th Congressional District.

Miller recently lost to Democratic opponent Brian Poindexter in Tuesday’s midterms.

Gonzalez’s impeachment vote particularly enraged the Ohio Republican Party, whose leaders censured him and called for his resignation in May 2021.

Gonzalez, a former professional football player, finished off his time in the House by voting in favor of establishing the independent commission on Jan. 6 and even supported holding Steve Bannon in contempt for refusing to cooperate with the Jan. 6 investigative panel.

Former Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler (Wash.) lost in a crowded primary to Trump-backed Republican Joe Kent in 2022 following her support for Trump’s impeachment. Herrera Beutler was condemned by Washington state’s Republican Party at the time for her impeachment vote.

Kent eventually lost to Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D) in the race to lead Washington’s 3rd Congressional District. On Tuesday, Gluesenkamp Perez defeated her Republican challenger in the midterms, retaining her 3rd District seat.

Former Rep. John Katko (N.Y.) announced his retirement close to one year after he voted to impeach Trump. He also planned to step down as chair of the Republican Governance Group, a caucus of moderate House Republicans he’d led since 2017.

Katko joined the HillEast Group, a Washington-based lobbying and communications firm, in January 2023 as a senior adviser. The firm was hired by the NHL to lobby on issues related to league event security.

Rep. Claudia Tenney (R) succeeded Katko in leading New York’s 24th Congressional District. She earned Trump’s endorsement in the 2026 midterms and defended her seat in an election cycle that saw the GOP losing in competitive elections, particularly in red strongholds.

Kinzinger was among the members of this group to receive the most backlash for his impeachment vote and his subsequent tenure of the House panel investigating Jan. 6.

He announced his retirement in October 2021, following a redistricting effort that would have pitted him against Trump-backed Rep. Darin LaHood (R).

LaHood won reelection Tuesday in the race to represent Illinois’s 16th Congressional District.

Since his departure from the House, Kinzinger has been a vocal critic of Trump and said he saw “ failure after failure ” when looking at the president’s first 100 days back in office in 2025.

Former Rep. Peter Meijer (Mich.) lost in the primaries to Trump-backed Republican John Gibbs in 2022.

At the time, Meijer and Kinzinger condemned the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee for running an ad they said boosted Gibbs, who supported Trump’s unfounded claims of fraud in the 2020 presidential election.

Gibbs ultimately lost to Democratic challenger Rep. Hillary Scholten to lead Michigan’s 3rd Congressional District. Scholten easily won reelection in Tuesday’s midterms.

Meijer launched a Senate bid in 2023 to replace former Sen. Debbie Stabenow (D), but he withdrew. Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) eventually earned the GOP nomination, though he lost to Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D).

Newhouse was one of two lawmakers to retain his House seat following the impeachment votes.

In 2022, Newhouse defeated Trump-endorsed Loren Culp, a former police chief, in the GOP primary to lead Washington’s 4th Congressional District. He also defeated Republican Jerrod Sessler, a former NASCAR driver who was in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 6, 2021.

Recently, Newhouse signed on to a letter urging Trump to cancel his Russian oil deal . The group of bipartisan lawmakers implored the administration to “not issue further general licenses that reopen Russian energy transactions and restore revenue to the Kremlin’s war chest.”

He announced he would not be seeking reelection in December 2025.

Former Rep. Tom Rice (S.C.) was the first Republican to lose reelection after voting to impeach Trump in 2021.

He lost to Rep. Russell Fry (R), who defended his House seat Tuesday despite major GOP losses in South Carolina — particularly Sen. Darline Graham’s (R) stunning loss to Annie Andrews (D) in the state’s Senate race.

Rice made headlines for refusing to back Harris in the 2024 presidential election, instead saying he would vote for neither her nor Trump.

“Donald Trump is a proven liar and a fraud and thief and a sexual predator. Everyone now knows that,” Rice told The Hill at the time. “But the thing that absolutely disqualifies him from office is his disregard for the Constitution.”

Former Rep. Fred Upton (Mich.) announced his retirement at the end of his term in 2022. He broke a record in the House by being the only lawmaker in the country’s history to vote to impeach two presidents: Trump and former President Clinton.

Though a moderate Republican while in the House, he broke away from the GOP on his impeachment vote and on a national red flag law opposed by most Republican lawmakers.

He also endorsed Harris in 2024 over Trump, calling the president “unfit” to lead again.

“That day was a tragedy for our democracy and Donald Trump is wrong to claim that everything he did was ‘totally appropriate’ when he directly jeopardized the peaceful transition from one administration to the next,” Upton wrote in a statement at the time, referring to the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol.

His district in Michigan is now represented by Rep. Debbie Dingell (D) who handily won reelection this midterm cycle.

Valadao was the last of the group to run for reelection. He is projected to lose to progressive challenger Villegas in the race affected by California’s redistricting effort.

He was one of two to win reelection in 2022, but unlike his other pro-impeachment Republicans, Trump did not endorse a challenger in Valadao’s GOP primary.

Valadao served in the House from 2013 to 2019 before being ousted by former Rep. TJ Cox (D). In a 2021 rematch, Valadao won back his seat and voted to impeach Trump one day after being sworn in.

The outgoing lawmaker notably did not attend the GOP’s first-ever midterm convention in September, electing to stay home instead.

With Valadao and Newhouse exiting the lower chamber, there were will no longer be any Republicans who voted to impeach Trump left in the House.

articles.title: Iowa Democrat who quit race wins seat anyway
articles.summary: The Democratic nominee in an Iowa state House District race won his race on Wednesday afternoon, despite suspending his bid in September for health reasons, amid a historic election night Democrats have declared a “blue tsunami.” Eric Armstrong, a retired railroad executive, defeated GOP candidate Keith Jones by about 9 percentage points and around 865…
articles.body:
The Democratic nominee in an Iowa state House District race won his race on Wednesday afternoon, despite suspending his bid in September for health reasons, amid a historic election night Democrats have declared a “ blue tsunami .”

Eric Armstrong, a retired railroad executive, defeated GOP candidate Keith Jones by about 9 percentage points and around 865 votes, according to The Associated Press.

Armstrong will fill the state House seat previously held by Josh Turek, the Democratic state lawmaker who won the Iowa Senate race on Tuesday evening.

In a Facebook post on Sept. 7, Armstrong announced he would be stepping away from his campaign, effective immediately, to address “some personal health issues.”

“Because I must prioritize my health and recovery at this time, I am stepping down from my campaign, effective immediately,” he wrote in the post. “This was a deeply difficult choice. However, I know it is the right one.

“Our District deserves a representative who can give 100 percent of their energy to this race,” the Democrat continued. “Right now, I must focus on healing so that I can continue to serve our community in other ways in the future.”

Armstrong told The New York Times in a phone call Wednesday morning that he would do his “best to represent” his district.

“But I still have health issues, that’s what I’m struggling with,” he added.

Democrats scored major wins in statewide races across the country, gaining control of both chambers of Congress and flipping state legislatures across the country. The party turned the gubernatorial and Senate seats in Texas blue for the first time in decades and secured notable victories in red states like Kansas, South Carolina and Florida.

In Iowa, Turek bested his GOP opponent in the Senate race and Democrat Rob Sand won the state’s gubernatorial race.

articles.title: How the Mississippi Senate Race Became a Nail-Biter
articles.summary: Eyes are on the closely divided race, where Democratic challenger Scott Colom is leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by a razor-thin margin.
articles.body:
As Democrats are celebrating a historic blue wave , eyes are on the Senate race in deep-red Mississippi, where the Democratic candidate led the Republican incumbent by a razor-thin margin of 1,138 votes as of Wednesday evening.

The Associated Press has not yet called the race because it is so close, with Democratic challenger Scott Colom ahead by about 0.1%—he has so far earned 49% of the vote compared to Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith's 48.9%, with 96% of votes counted. It's a stunning nail-biter of a race that, in the weeks leading up to Election Day, polls had suggested would likely be won by the Republican incumbent by a narrow margin.

"I can't recall the last time it's been this close for a statewide Senate contest—or a statewide election in general," says Aaron Hitefield, an assistant professor of political science at Mississippi State University. "It's unprecedented for [Mississippi] to be this competitive for Democrats particularly, certainly in the last 40 years."

Political experts say it could take a few days before the outcome of the race becomes clear.

If Colom, a district attorney, wins the race, it would be the first time that Mississippi voters have elected a Democrat to represent them in the U.S. Senate since 1982. A Democratic victory would also be a remarkable shift in a state that President Donald Trump won by a nearly 23-point margin just two years ago.

Such an upset would cap off a string of staggering victories for Democrats, who have so far flipped seven seats in the upper chamber in this year's midterm elections, including in other staunchly red states like Texas and South Carolina .

Both candidates appeared to be optimistic that the election would ultimately go their way, though they also acknowledged that the race is still too close to call. Colom said in a statement early Wednesday morning, "I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat."

"The results are all trending in our direction," Colom said in a speech to his supporters on Election Night. "The reality is, though, we're not going to get the results tonight. I'm excited about our momentum, I'm excited about where we are."

Speaking to a crowd of her supporters on Election Night , Hyde-Smith said she was confident that she would hold her seat in the upper chamber.

"We still don't have all the votes in, so we're not calling all of it tonight, but we're in a very good lead and I assure you, I will continue to be your U.S. Senator," she said .

When asked about Hyde-Smith's speech at a press conference on Wednesday, Colom replied , "Bless her heart."

When will we know who won the Mississippi Senate race?

It is possible that the winner of the Senate contest may not be determined until the end of the week—or even next week.

The state has five business days after Election Day to count affidavit ballots. An individual would turn in such a ballot, which is also called a provisional ballot, in a situation in which they believe they're eligible and registered to vote but are unable to cast a standard ballot—for instance, if their name is not in their local polling place's records. These votes are only counted once election workers verify the individual's information. Mississippi also permits mail-in ballots that arrive within five days after Election Day, so long as they were postmarked by Election Day, to be counted.

All this means that it's possible the race may not be called until a week after Election Day, says Emily Ommundsen, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Mississippi.

"Because of the razor-thin margins we currently see, I don't expect any results to be called before then," Ommundsen says.

How did the Mississippi Senate race become such a tight contest?

The tight race in Mississippi is one of many that illustrate the extremely challenging political environment Republicans have faced this year.

Historically, the party in the White House loses seats in midterm elections, and that pressure on Republicans was compounded in this election cycle because of historically low approval for Trump driven in large part by the economy, as well as the war in Iran.

Ommundsen says that, while ballots are still being counted, the result in Mississippi, so far, "is consistent with trends that we saw nationally."

"Nearly all counties that had a Senate election on the ballot moved towards the left compared to how they voted in 2024," she says, though she notes that there are some exceptions. "Mississippi just happens to be one of those elections that was closer and perhaps more ripe for a flip."

Hitefield likens this year's midterms to "a referendum on the President," adding that "Democrats were turning out to oppose the President and to oppose the President's policies."

But he cautions that the close contest in Mississippi is not necessarily a sign that the deep-red state is turning blue or even purple. It's possible, he says, that Republican voters didn't cast their ballots for a Democrat, and instead stayed home.

"I wouldn't necessarily read in, long story short, to Mississippi becoming a Georgia—you know, being a fully competitive every election state," Hitefield says. "But I think it's certainly moving toward a state that you shouldn't sleep on when it comes to electoral competitiveness."

Hitefield also says that there's a lot of "voter apathy" within the Republican party with regards to Hyde-Smith, and she hasn't performed as well as Mississippi's other Republican Senator, Roger Wicker, in past elections. Wicker won his re-election bid in 2024 by a more than 25-point margin . Hyde-Smith, meanwhile, won her re-election fight in 2020 by about 10 points .

Hitefield adds that Hyde-Smith had some "gaffes" during the campaign, when she made some remarks about the rising cost of living that some voters felt were dismissive. For instance, when asked about soaring costs, including beef prices, during an interview with WLOX in February, Hyde-Smith applauded the passing of Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill and went on to say, "It is on everybody's mind. It is certainly me at my house. And you know, you have so many proteins to choose from. And all commodities go through peaks and valleys."

National polling ahead of Election Day indicated that an overwhelming majority of American voters felt that the economy was a crucial issue for them heading into this year's midterms.

Colom's campaign jumped on Hyde-Smith's remark, releasing an ad in which people objected to Hyde-Smith's comment, including one who said in the video, "Pick another protein? Sh**, I'd rather pick another Senator instead." The ad racked up more than 7.5 million views on Colom's X account .

Ommundsen points out that Hyde-Smith didn't make many public campaign appearances in this year's election cycle; one of the few appearances the Senator made was last week, when she gave very brief remarks at a rally the President held for her in Mississippi.

Hitefield says Hyde-Smith didn't "do the groundwork necessary to run a successful campaign" in this election cycle.

"I think that it was a real mistake by her campaign, regardless of what the outcome looks like at the end of this," Hitefield says. "Even if she does win, she didn't do, really, what she needed to win with any sort of safety. I think that's something [where] if she does win, she'll need to think about, moving forward, how to strategize more effectively."

Colom, on the other hand, ran a "successful campaign" and generated "so much voter excitement," Hitefield says—so much so that it stirred "this groundswell of hopes within the Democratic party that this seat could be flipped."

If Colom wins, he would also become the first Black Senator from Mississippi since the 19th century—the last time the state sent a Black lawmaker to the upper chamber was during Reconstruction in the aftermath of the Civil War.

"It would be an unprecedented outcome when it comes to the history of Mississippi," Hitefield says.

articles.title: Legal challenges expected in tight Mississippi Senate race
articles.summary: The winning candidate may not be identified for up to another three weeks with Democrat Scott Colom ahead by a narrow margin.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — This week's blue wave that captured Senate seats in traditionally red states like Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Texas may yet claim Mississippi , where Democrat Scott Colom was ahead of incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by a narrow margin.

But don't expect a final answer any time soon. The winning candidate may not be identified for up to another three weeks, said Scott Tranter, director of data science for NewsNation partner Decision Desk HQ.

Although Colom was ahead by nearly 2,000 votes with 95% of ballots counted, election officials must still process thousands of mail-in and provisional ballots within prescribed deadlines. The state must certify results by Nov. 13.

"We're not sure how they're going to cure those absentee ballots and process all those," Tranter told "The Hill" on Wednesday.

Observers expect legal challenges from both sides because of the narrow margin, which could further delay the declaration of a winner.

The dead heat between Colom and Hyde-Smith was not anticipated in Mississippi, a conservative-leaning state that President Trump, a Republican, carried by more than 20 points in 2024. Voters have not elected a Democrat to the Senate there since 1982.

But a handful of red states rejected Republican candidates Tuesday in a movement that is seen as a rebuke of Trump administration policies, including tariffs, immigration enforcement and the war in Iran.

articles.title: Texas state rep calls on Abbott to curb Hinojosa’s power before inauguration
articles.summary: Texas state Rep. Brian Harrison (R) on Wednesday called on Gov. Greg Abbott (R) to curb Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa’s (D) power before she is sworn in next year. “We still have total power in Texas, and we must act like it by using the remaining ten weeks to restore separation of powers and limit the…
articles.body:
Texas state Rep. Brian Harrison (R) on Wednesday called on Gov. Greg Abbott (R) to curb Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa’s (D) power before she is sworn in next year.

“We still have total power in Texas, and we must act like it by using the remaining ten weeks to restore separation of powers and limit the emergency powers that Governor-Elect Hinojosa is set to inherit, which would allow her to destroy liberty in Texas by executive fiat,” Harrison wrote in a lengthy post on the social platform X .

Harrison wrote that Hinojosa should not have “unchecked emergency powers” and that “the urgency is undeniable… and inaction is intolerable.” He claimed that Hinojosa will “inherit the powers of a DICTATOR.”

“Due to the absurd (and almost certainly unconstitutional) Texas emergency powers laws, Gov. Hinojosa will literally have the power to modify laws, ignore laws, or create and enforce laws – including criminal laws – on a whim!” Harrison said.

He called on the Texas state House to pass HB911, a bill he filed in 2022 against “never ending emergency powers.” Harrison cited the bill’s text, which states that legislative bodies “allowing a single executive branch official to both write and enforce laws is the biggest threat to our constitutional system of divided government and should be opposed irrespective of which political party runs the executive branch.”

“We have TEN WEEKS LEFT to protect Texas from near total Democrat rule,” Harrison’s post concludes. “I encourage every elected Republican in Texas to join my demand for Gov. Abbott to call a special session. The future of liberty in America is literally on the line in Texas, and Texans deserve leadership that acts accordingly.”

Hinojosa defeated Abbott with her 52.78 percent of the vote to his 45.66 percent, according to The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ . Abbott conceded and told supporters that he would “assist her and her team in a period of transition.” Her win flipped the governor’s mansion blue for the first time since former Gov. Ann Richards won in 1990.

Hinojosa will likely enter her new role with more powers than anticipated on the campaign trail, The Houston Chronicle reported. She could also face roadblocks, as Texas Republicans have vowed to “hold the line” against the state Democrat’s agenda.

Former Texas state House speaker Dade Phelan (R) told the outlet that he expects Hinojosa to accomplish her plans even with GOP opposition, as they don’t hold a majority big enough in the state Senate “to govern with an iron fist.”

“Things have to occur,” Phelan told the Chronicle. “They don’t have every lever of government like they are accustomed to.”

The strong night for Democrats in Texas did not apply solely to Hinojosa and Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas), as Democratic state Rep. Vikki Goodwin defeated Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick (R), and Democrats won the races for state attorney general, comptroller, railroad commissioner and agriculture commissioner.

Democrats also won the Texas state House, concluding the 24-year run Republicans held in both state Legislature chambers.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Crushing midterm rebuke' and 'Trumped'
articles.summary: The Democrats sweep in the US midterm elections is the focus of Thursday's papers.
articles.body:
The fallout from the US midterm elections features on most of the morning's front pages, including the Financial Times , which says Americans delivered a "crushing rebuke" to Donald Trump, after a campaign dominated by the spiralling cost of living. The Daily Mail agrees, arguing voters passed a "damning verdict" on the president because they were "enraged" by high inflation and rising fuel prices.

The Times says Mr Trump has entered a "lame duck period" after a series of "history-making moments", including the election of America's first Muslim senator. According to the Daily Mirror , Abdul El-Sayed won in Michigan "despite a vile smear campaign" after voters grew sick of the president's "bullying" and "narcissism".

With the headline, "Vance Turns On Trump", the Daily Telegraph highlights how the US vice president has blamed the Iran war for the Republicans' humiliation. It says JD Vance is now "desperately trying to distance himself" from the conflict, in what's described as a "first move towards a possible 2028 White House run". The Guardian warns that Donald Trump is "psychologically ill-equipped" to deal with the spotlight that is leaving him to focus on potential candidates. But the paper suggests that such a shift could "eat away" at what it calls the president's "cult-like dominance" of the Republican party.

The Sun says the FBI is to search lock-ups in Hollywood, rented by the father of the Duchess of Sussex, as part of an investigation into allegations of child sexual abuse. The paper says Thomas Markle's son was interviewed by agents after he informed them about the two storage units. Markle has called the claims against him "sick lies".

The Daily Express features the concerns of residents in the North Yorkshire village of Linton-on-Ouse, where the government plans to house more than 1,200 asylum seekers on a former RAF base. Writing in the paper, the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, says anyone who thinks families will carry on as normal when hundreds of men are camped at the end of their road has never had to walk a teenage daughter home in the dark. Ministers say the site is designed to be as self-sufficient as possible to reduce the impact on the local community.

images.caption: Almost all the front pages carry the results of the US midterm elections, where President Donald Trump's Republican Party is suffering heavy defeats and will lose control of Congress. "Crushing midterm rebuke to Trump" is the Financial Times' verdict, embedding a tally of the results so far - which show the Democrats winning majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives. "Anger over cost of living spurs Democratic blue wave" the paper says, providing its business-focused audience a taste of the market reaction by reporting "oil prices tumble and tech hyperscalers' shares surge".

articles.title: Raman ousts Bass as Los Angeles mayor
articles.summary: Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman (D) is projected to become the next mayor of Los Angeles after ousting embattled Mayor Karen Bass (D) after one term, according to Decision Desk HQ. The race was called Wednesday evening with Raman leading by about 26,000 votes—roughly 3 percent—out of 784,262 votes cast, per DDHQ. Raman…
articles.body:
Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman (D) is projected to become the next mayor of Los Angeles after ousting embattled Mayor Karen Bass (D) after one term, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The race was called Wednesday evening with Raman leading by about 26,000 votes—roughly 3 percent—out of 784,262 votes cast, per DDHQ.

Raman defeated Bass after the two advanced from the June 2 nonpartisan jungle primary, ousting former reality TV star Spencer Pratt from the race.

The council member was a late entry to the mayoral race in February. A former Bass ally, she differentiated her campaign from the mayor’s incumbency by focusing on her handling of several issues, including fallout from 2025’s devastating Palisades and Eaton fires, homelessness, reform of the Los Angeles Police Department and affordable housing, and what she would do differently.

Raman was first elected in 2020, defeating incumbent City Council member David Ryu. She secured several endorsements in her mayoral campaign, including from the Sierra Club, Unite Here Local 11, LA Forward, the Eastside Padres Contra la Privatización and the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) Los Angeles chapter, of which she is a member.

Though she campaigned on being independent from DSA in her decisionmaking on the City Council, her political affiliation makes her the city’s first socialist mayor. It also gives the organization another victory with a democratic socialist leading a major American city, following New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s (D) victory last year.

Long before the primary, when Raman faced off against democratic socialist the Rev. Rae Huang, lawyer Job Harriman was the last Socialist Party candidate in the City of Angels to run for mayor in 1911.

Harriman lost support before the election following the bombing of the Los Angeles Times building, which was linked to two union members whom Harriman represented in court, according to the Museum of the New Llano Colony .

articles.title: Gluesenkamp Perez holds on to Washington House seat

Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) is projected to defend her House seat and defeat her GOP challenger, John Braun, in the race for Washington’s 3rd District, according to Decision Desk HQ. Gluesenkamp Perez currently stands at about 55 percent of the vote to her Republican rival’s 44 percent with 81 percent reporting, per DDHQ. Gluesenkamp…
articles.body:
Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) is projected to defend her House seat and defeat her GOP challenger, John Braun, in the race for Washington’s 3rd District, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Gluesenkamp Perez currently stands at about 55 percent of the vote to her Republican rival’s 44 percent with 81 percent reporting, per DDHQ.

Gluesenkamp Perez holding on to her district, which voted for President Trump in 2024 per The Downballot , marks a key win for Democrats as they look to clinch control of the House. The nonpartisan political handicapper Cook Political Report rated the race between Gluesenkamp Perez and Braun as leaning Democratic .

The Washington Democrat was first elected in 2022 , when she defeated Republican Joe Kent, a retired Green Beret and CIA paramilitary officer, and flipped the seat held by former Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler (R). Herrera Beutler lost the 2022 GOP primary to Kent, who went on to serve in the Trump administration but later resigned over U.S. military operations in Iran.

Trump endorsed Braun, a Navy veteran and owner of the vehicle manufacturer Braun Northwest, against Gluesenkamp Perez in April. He framed Gluesenkamp Perez as an extremist opposed to his policy agenda.

“John is running against Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a true Radical Left Extremist with a Track Record that REEKS, and who does not represent the Values of Southwestern Washington,” Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.

Gluesenkamp Perez, a moderate, has come under scrutiny from fellow Democrats for crossing the aisle to support legislation opposed by her party .

articles.title: Democrats flip open Arizona House seat
articles.summary: Former Democratic state Rep. Amish Shah is projected to defeat Republican former NFL kicker Jay Feely to win Arizona’s 1st District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), flipping a competitive seat Shah narrowly lost two years earlier. Shah led with 52.5 percent of the vote to Feely’s 45.5 percent with over 95 percent of votes…
articles.body:
Former Democratic state Rep. Amish Shah is projected to defeat Republican former NFL kicker Jay Feely to win Arizona’s 1st District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) , flipping a competitive seat Shah narrowly lost two years earlier.

Shah led with 52.5 percent of the vote to Feely’s 45.5 percent with over 95 percent of votes reported when the race was called, per DDHQ.

Shah will succeed Rep. David Schweikert (R-Ariz.), who beat Shah by 3.8 percentage points in 2024. Schweikert launched an unsuccessful bid for governor this year, creating an opening for Democrats to compete in a more favorable political environment without facing an incumbent.

The district — which includes Scottsdale, Paradise Valley, Fountain Hills, Cave Creek and parts of northeast Phoenix — backed President Trump by roughly 3 points in 2024 but also supported Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego by about 5 points that year. The district was considered one of the most competitive in the country this cycle.

Shah entered the closing days of the race as the favorite. Cook Political Report shifted the race from “toss up” to “lean Democrat” in September, while DDHQ rated the district as “likely Democrat,” giving Shah a 76 percent chance of winning as of Sunday.

An emergency room physician and former Arizona state lawmaker, Shah secured the Democratic nomination over former broadcast journalist Marlene Galán-Woods, who was backed by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC).

Shah pointed to the DCCC’s support of his primary opponent as evidence that he would be an independent voice in Congress and not fall in line behind party leaders. He also emphasized his bipartisan record in the state legislature and touted his support from former GOP state House Speaker Rusty Bowers.

The Democrat sought to contrast his record with his opponent’s relationship with Trump, arguing Feely owed his primary victory to the president. Feely initially ran in the more GOP-friendly 5th District but switched after the president urged him to do so and gave him an endorsement.

Feely, a political newcomer, became a sports commentator after playing 14 NFL seasons, including four with the Arizona Cardinals. He argued his relationship with Trump would benefit Arizona and painted Shah as too liberal for the district. Feely largely defended Trump’s agenda but broke with the president over his administration’s proposed cuts to Arizona’s Colorado River allocation.

articles.title: Cruz warns ‘Texans will be hurt’ after ‘blue tsunami’
articles.summary: Texas Sen. Ted Cruz (R) issued a stark warning on Wednesday evening after Democrats flipped a Texas Senate seat and the governor’s mansion in the midterm elections. In a lengthy statement shared on social media, the GOP senator said that “Texans will be hurt” by the blue tsunami that swept across the state and country…
articles.body:
Texas Sen. Ted Cruz (R) issued a stark warning on Wednesday evening after Democrats flipped a Texas Senate seat and the governor’s mansion in the midterm elections.

In a lengthy statement shared on social media, the GOP senator said that “Texans will be hurt” by the blue tsunami that swept across the state and country on Tuesday.

“Their assault on business will make Texas a much less attractive place to start or grow a small business,” he wrote. “Texas will become more like California if they succeed in halting all new investment into AI.”

State Reps. James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa became the first Democrats elected to the U.S. Senate and Texas governor’s office in decades in a stunning upset for Republicans in the Lone Star State on Election Day.

“Texas is blue. That is a hard sentence to utter,” Cruz wrote. “But Texas, today at least, is blue. As we sit here today, I am the only statewide elected Republican who remains in Texas. That’s not something I ever thought I would say.”

The Texas Republican and other prominent GOP leaders, including President Trump, backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) in the Senate race. Talarico defeated the Republican nominee by over 12 percentage points, according to Decision Desk HQ .

Cruz said he spoke with the Democratic victor following his win on Tuesday evening to congratulate him “on his very impressive victory.”

“It was a pleasant conversation, and I told him that I looked forward to working with him to try to benefit Texas,” he said.

The Republican senator said his party will need to do “two things” in the next two years under new Democratic control of both chambers of Congress: “fight the madness” and “rebuild.”

In a Wednesday op-ed in The Wall Street Journal, outgoing GOP Texas Sen. John Cornyn urged his party to refocus on winning principles following their losses in the Lone Star State and nationwide.

“This week’s beat-down wasn’t only foreseeable, it was foreseen,” the Republican wrote, citing shortcomings in GOP candidates’ appeals to voters and the Trump administration’s ability to deliver on 2024 campaign promises.

However, both Cornyn and Cruz expressed optimism that the GOP will regain the seats lost to Democrats this cycle.

Cruz wrote in his Wednesday evening post that he was “filled with hope and optimism.”

“Texas will be red again,” he continued. “We have not suddenly become a bunch of tofu-eating, gun-banning, tutu-wearing pinko commie liberals. That ain’t us. Texas is still Texas.”

articles.title: Billionaire Leon Black sues Rep. Robert Garcia, alleging defamation over Epstein comments
articles.summary: Garcia is poised to be the next chair of the House Oversight Committee, which has subpoenaed Black as part of its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein.
articles.body: Billionaire Leon Black filed a defamation lawsuit Wednesday against Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, which has spearheaded a Jeffrey Epstein investigation. Black has been the target of subpoenas from the Republican-led committee, which unanimously voted in September to hold him in contempt over his refusal to comply with those subpoenas. Black, a former Wall Street private equity investor who had a business relationship with Epstein, sued Garcia in the Southern District of New York, alleging he “has knowingly and willfully lied about Leon Black and defamed him.” The suit cites comments from Garcia that Black was “at the center” and “directly involved” with Epstein’s crimes. A spokesperson for Garcia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit. Garcia said in a statement in September in response to a lawsuit Black filed against the committee that Black had “funded Epstein’s abuse and trafficking of women,” adding: “Multiple women have also accused Black of sexual assault. His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable.” In a statement about the lawsuit against Garcia on Wednesday, a spokesperson for Black wrote that “he has never abused a woman; he has never been with an underage woman; he has never been involved with sex trafficking; and, he never paid Epstein for women.” With Democrats set to take control of the House in January, Garcia is poised to become the new chair of the Oversight Committee. Black stepped down from the hedge fund he co-founded, Apollo Global Management, in 2021 after the firm conducted an independent review of his ties to Epstein. The review found that Black, who has denied wrongdoing tied to Epstein, wasn’t involved in Epstein’s criminal activities. Black sat for a voluntary closed-door transcribed interview with the House Oversight Committee over the summer but left before it was over. Lawmakers on the committee issued subpoenas to compel him to answer questions they said he wasn’t answering, but Black didn’t show up for a later deposition. He then sued the committee to block the subpoenas for his appearance and nondisclosure agreements tied to Epstein. The case is still being litigated. The House later voted to hold Black in contempt of Congress. Reuters reported that the Justice Department said Sept. 16 in a statement that the “US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia will review the referral of Mr. Black carefully and will not hesitate to pursue additional cases where the evidence supports.” No charges have been filed against Black.

articles.title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
articles.summary: The vice-president's blunt assessment of Republican election defeat marked one of the sharpest breaks with a sitting president in recent memory.
articles.body:
Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.

In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election .

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."

In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate .

Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.

But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.

Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.

It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.

Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.

It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.

"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."

Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.

That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.

Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.

Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."

The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.

The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.

Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.

It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.

Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.

The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.

The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).

Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.

articles.title: Scott Wiener prevails in race to succeed retiring Pelosi
articles.summary: Democrat Scott Wiener is poised to win the California seat to succeed Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), after his opponent San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan conceded Wednesday evening in a statement according to local Fox affiliate KTVU. Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s partner, has not called the race yet, but Wiener leads Chan by about…
articles.body:
Democrat Scott Wiener is poised to win the California seat to succeed Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), after his opponent San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan conceded Wednesday evening in a statement according to local Fox affiliate KTVU .

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s partner, has not called the race yet, but Wiener leads Chan by about 11 points with 62 percent of votes reported.

Wiener, a California state senator for more than 10 years, beat out Chan for California’s 11th Congressional District in what was expected to be a close race . Polling in recent weeks showed Wiener with a slight edge.

Pelosi, who is retiring after nearly four decades in the House, endorsed Chan , though Wiener also received high-profile endorsements from California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D), California State Treasurer Fiona Ma (D) and the San Francisco Chronicle.

Wiener will represent nearly all of San Francisco, where he has lived since 1997 after growing up in New Jersey.

As a state senator since 2016, Wiener represented San Francisco and northern San Mateo County and served as chair of the Standing Committee on Elections and Constitutional Amendments and the Select Committee on Bay Area Public Transit. He also served on the Transportation, Judiciary and Privacy, Digital Technologies, and Consumer Protection Private Safety committees.

The progressive lawmaker authored more than 100 bills that became law. His policies often focused on housing affordability, public transportation, LGBTQ rights and climate.

Wiener gained national attention for proposing some of the first safety regulations for artificial intelligence in 2024.

Prior to his time in the California Senate, Wiener served on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, along with spending about 15 years practicing law at the San Francisco City Attorney’s Office and in private practice.

After attending Harvard University, Wiener also was a law clerk for Justice Alan Handler on the New Jersey Supreme Court.

articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday called on Congress to pass the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent, after the day’s “ridiculous” early sunset.

“Too bad the Senate has not yet approved the Sunshine Protection Act or, the ‘I Don’t Want to Change My Clocks Anymore Act,'” he wrote on Truth Social . “It’s so dark outside, so early (Sunset was 5:06 P.M., and it was dark by 5:31 P.M. — Isn’t that ridiculous?). Just a few days ago it was so nice and sunny at this same time.”

“In addition, everyone’s been running around changing their clocks all over the place,” Trump continued. “I didn’t want to make a big deal out of this prior to the Election because I didn’t want to have certain Senators lose their Race, in a landslide, but it is too bad they can’t get it done.”

The president concluded that the “House sent it over to the Senate with great bipartisan support, numerous times (308-117), but the Senate didn’t take it up. We have far bigger priorities, but I will keep fighting for this.”

Trump has been a big proponent of the bill, which the House passed earlier this year but the Senate has yet to pick it up. The bill would end the semiannual clock change.

He previously said the clock change was “ridiculous” during a rally in Mississippi last month, adding that it “drives everyone crazy, which nobody wants to do anymore.” The president also pointed to data that shows how less crime is committed when it’s brighter outside in the early evening, going further to say that it costs the U.S. “a fortune” and is “bad for Crime.”

Reps. Mary Gay Scanlon (D-Pa.) and Pat Harrigan (R-N.C.) introduced the Sunshine for Our Kids Act to establish a permanent standard time always seen from November to March. They noted that more sunlight in the evenings would leave mornings dark for children going to school and commuters leaving for work.

Staunch Trump supporter Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), however, has been a vocal opponent against the legislation. He argued on the social platform X in October that while “no one likes changing the clock, me included,” Congress has made daylight saving time permanent before and repealed it “once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter.”

An AP-NORC poll released last month found that 12 percent of U.S. adults favor the twice-a-year change and 47 percent oppose it, with 40 percent who say they are indifferent about it. Fifty-six percent said they prefer year-round daylight saving time, and 42 percent prefer standard daylight time all year.
